title: Is Wastewater Surveillance Predictive during the Endemic Phase of Respiratory Disease? An Analysis Based on Clinical, Wastewater, and Digital Search Data in Detroit, Michigan
abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has emerged as a major public health innovation catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic. However, its potential remains underexplored during and after COVID-19’s transition to endemicity. This study evaluates WBE’s potential to identify the COVID-19 pandemic-to-endemic transition and to provide early warnings across multiple surveillance systems for influenza A (IAV) and B (IBV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 in the postpandemic era. We monitored SARS-CoV-2 N1 concentrations in wastewater from April 8, 2020, and July 31, 2025, generating the earliest and longest-running wastewater dataset in Detroit, MI. A peak identification method was implemented to identify the pandemic-to-endemic transition by comparing the frequency of N1 concentration peaks between phases. During the endemic phase, from October 1, 2022, and March 31, 2025, we monitored RSV, IAV, IBV, and SARS-CoV-2 in Detroit’s wastewater. Pearson correlations were implemented to quantify the associations between wastewater concentrations and clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological data. Time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) was used to examine temporal dynamics among these datasets and identify the earliest emerging data for each disease and time lags. Extensive literature studies were conducted to elucidate the time-lag mechanisms for each disease, embracing the TLCC results. Random forest models were established to predict clinical cases based on WBE datasets. This was among the first studies using WBE-based approaches to identify pandemic-to-endemic transition of SARS-CoV-2. The relationships of wastewater data to traditional clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological surveillance data were systematically analyzed during the endemic phase of these respiratory diseases. This study demonstrates the predictive value of WBE during the endemic phase, providing early warnings and predictions for seasonal respiratory diseases, including COVID-19, influenza, and flu-like disease.

title: Evaluation of the Performance of the BD VeritorTM System for Detection of Acute Respiratory Viruses: Comparison with RT-PCR in Mali
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the need for rapid and accurate diagnosis of respiratory viral infections and reinforced the importance of integrated respiratory virus surveillance systems. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) provide timely results but may show limited sensitivity compared with molecular assays. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the BD VeritorTM System for Rapid Detection of Respiratory Viruses for detecting respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Influenza A, and Influenza B in Mali, using multiplex real-time RT-PCR as the reference standard. A total of 1202 nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swab specimens collected between March 2020 and March 2022 from suspected respiratory infection cases were analyzed. Samples were tested using the BD VeritorTM rapid antigen assay and compared with the ViroQ® SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB/RSV multiplex RT-PCR assay performed on the LightCycler® 480 II system. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and Cohen’s kappa coefficient. The BD VeritorTM assay demonstrated consistently high specificity (>91%) for all viral targets, whereas sensitivity remained low, ranging from 21.05% to 30.43%. Positive predictive values ranged from 24.78% to 46.15%, while negative predictive values remained above 83%. Agreement with RT-PCR was low (κ = 0.14–0.24), indicating limited concordance between the two methods. The reduced sensitivity observed may partly be explained by low viral loads, prolonged frozen storage of samples before antigen testing, and the complex epidemiological context associated with the co-circulation of respiratory viruses during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although the BD VeritorTM assay may provide useful support for rapid clinical orientation and triage in resource-limited settings, negative results should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed by RT-PCR whenever possible.

title: HVSnp: A manually curated database of human SNPS associated with viral infections.
abstract: We developed the "HVSnp: Human Viruses SNP-related database, a curated database". HVSnp is exclusive to the human SNPs studied and related to viral diseases, with manually mined and curated information from public SNP databases and scientific articles. We used MySQL (version 8.0) due to the easy management and the Looker Studio online availability. Among the output information, we have SNP identification, reference, alternative, and risk alleles, chromosome, gene, and gene function, summary, among others. In total, HVSnp contains eighteen viral diseases and 2020 records: Adenovirus (17 SNPs), Chikungunya (7), COVID-19 (314), Cytomegalovirus (54), Dengue (62), Epstein-Barr (54), Hepatitis A (3), Hepatitis B (380), Hepatitis C (166), Herpes (8), Human immunodeficiency virus (479), Papillomavirus (87), Influenza (74), Measles (68), Respiratory syncytial virus (50), Sars-CoV (80), West Nile (68), and Zika (49). As one SNP can be associated with more than one virus, the number of unique SNPs is 1691 and 651 genes. HVSnp has supplementary information obtained in articles for the summary elaboration, which contains the most significant results described in the literature about a possible relationship between SNPs and viruses. The database is available at URL: https://lookerstudio.google.com/s/pGUC7m538gQ.

title: Respiratory Viruses in the Air of Shared Indoor Environments: Multi-Country Molecular Surveillance Across Europe (TwinAIR)
abstract: Indoor environments are the dominant setting for human exposure to respiratory viruses, yet routine molecular surveillance of indoor air remains rare outside single-site studies. Within the Horizon Europe TwinAIR project, a single harmonised workflow was applied to 102 indoor air samples (2000 L each) collected between October 2024 and February 2026 at ten pilot settings in Germany, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain, Greece and Sweden, covering university teaching rooms, school classrooms and staff rooms, healthcare-associated offices, workplace offices, an elderly care facility and public transport vehicles. Air was collected onto gelatine membrane filters with a Sartorius MD8 Airport sampler, total nucleic acid was extracted with the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit, and five targets—SARS-CoV-2, human adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus A/B, influenza A and rhinovirus—were quantified against target-specific standard curves as genome copies per cubic metre (GC/m3). At least one target was detected in 84 of 102 samples (82.4%; 95% CI 73.8–88.5). title: Nosocomial RSV-related in-hospital mortality in children
abstract: Background: According to the World Health Organization, the global burden of nosocomial infections is poorly characterized as surveillance systems are lacking.Nosocomial infections occur at higher rates in low-and lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) than in high-income countries (HICs).Current global RSV burden estimates are largely based on community-acquired infection.We aimed to characterize children with nosocomial RSV-related mortality and to understand the potential impact of RSV immunization strategies.Materials: RSV GOLD is a global registry of children younger than 5 years who died with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection.We compared clinical and demographic characteristics of children with nosocomial and community-acquired RSV in-hospital mortality.Results: We included 231 nosocomial and 931 community-acquired RSVrelated in-hospital from deaths from 65 countries.Age at death was similar for both groups (5.4 vs. 6 months).A higher proportion of nosocomial deaths had comorbidities (87% vs. 57%; P < 0.001) or was born preterm (46% vs. 24%; P < 0.001) than community-acquired deaths.The proportion of nosocomial deaths among all RSV deaths was lower in LMICs than in upper-middle-income countries (UMICs) and HICs (12% vs. 18% and 26%, respectively).Conclusions: This is the first global case series of children dying with nosocomial RSV infection.Future infant-targeted immunization strategies could prevent the majority of nosocomial RSV-related deaths.Although nosocomial RSV deaths are expected to occur at highest rates in LMICs, the number of reported nosocomial RSV deaths was low in these countries.Hospital-based surveillance is needed to capture the full burden of nosocomial RSV mortality in LMICs.
authors: Peter F. M. Van der Ven

title: Information Overload? Mapping the Influence of Digital and Information-Related Factors on Maternal Vaccine Hesitancy: A Scoping Review
abstract: Maternal vaccinations protects both the mother and the infant, however the uptake remains suboptimal, partly due to hesitancy. Our scoping review aims to identify and map the available evidence on factors associated with maternal vaccine hesitancy among pregnant women in high income countires. The vaccines that we will investigate are influenza (A and B), pertussis, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Furthermore, we will have a particular focus on information-related factors, including digital health literacy.

title: Comparative clinical, immunological, and pulmonary responses to virulent bovine respiratory syncytial virus infection in colostrum-fed, intranasally vaccinated calves
abstract: Abstract Objective To compare clinical, pulmonary, and immunologic responses to bovine respiratory syncytial virus (BRSV) challenge in colostrum-fed, BRSV-seropositive calves following administration of 2 commercially available intranasal vaccines. Methods 34 male Holstein calves (9 to 20 days old) were randomly assigned to receive vaccine A (Nasalgen; n = 17) or vaccine B (Inforce 3; 17). Nine weeks after vaccination, calves were challenged with virulent BRSV. Clinical observations were recorded daily. Arterial partial pressure of oxygen was measured on day 6 after challenge, and percentage pneumonic lung involvement was assessed at necropsy on day 8. Antibody responses and viral shedding were assessed. Results Clinical signs were infrequent and mild in both groups, and nasal shedding of BRSV was low. Median lung lesion scores were lower in calves receiving vaccine B than in calves receiving vaccine A (2.3% vs 4.6%). Arterial oxygen concentrations were numerically higher in vaccine B calves (median, 91.0 mm Hg) than in vaccine A calves (median, 82.8 mm Hg), although this difference was not significant. A greater proportion of vaccine B calves had Pao 2 values within the normal range (> 87.1 mm Hg) compared to vaccine A calves (12 of 17 [71%] vs 7 of 17 [41%]). Both vaccines induced anamnestic mucosal and systemic antibody responses. Conclusions Both vaccines were associated with minimal clinical disease following BRSV challenge. Clinical Relevance Results suggest a modest advantage of vaccine B with respect to pulmonary involvement and maintenance of arterial oxygenation under these experimental conditions.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association

title: Systems serology identifies differential pan-viral seroreactivity profiles associated with healthy aging and cancer
abstract: Abstract A viral exposure signature (VES) has previously been shown to predict the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in at-risk individuals through comprehensive serological profiling using the VirScan platform. Whether cumulative antimicrobial immune histories are associated with cancer status across multiple malignancies remains unknown. We applied high-throughput VirScan systems serology to characterize antibody reactivities against a comprehensive microbial peptide library in 359 participants, including 172 patients with cancer and 187 healthy individuals. To account for age-related immune remodeling, healthy participants were stratified into adults ( 80 years, including nonagenarians and centenarians). Differential Pan-viral Seroreactivity Profiles (DPSPs) were identified through an unbiased statistical workflow combining differential class comparison, feature selection, predictive modeling, cross-validation, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Distinct DPSPs discriminated healthy individuals from patients with cancer. The identified signatures comprised antibody reactivities against peptides derived predominantly from persistent herpesviruses, acute respiratory viruses and, consistently across multiple comparisons, human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV). Remarkably, healthy elderly individuals generally exhibited higher antibody titers than patients with cancer, whereas healthy adults showed the opposite pattern. These differential serological signatures supported accurate class prediction in several comparisons, indicating that cumulative antimicrobial immune histories differ according to health status after accounting for physiological immune aging. Our findings demonstrate that lifelong cumulative antimicrobial immune history generates reproducible serological signatures associated with healthy aging and cancer status. Although the present cross-sectional study does not establish causal biological protection, it identifies hypothesis-generating biomarkers that warrant validation in independent prospective cohorts and supports the potential value of comprehensive serological profiling for future cancer risk stratification.

These differential serological signatures supported accurate class prediction in several comparisons, indicating that cumulative antimicrobial immune histories differ according to health status after accounting for physiological immune aging. Our findings demonstrate that lifelong cumulative antimicrobial immune history generates reproducible serological signatures associated with healthy aging and cancer status. Although the present cross-sectional study does not establish causal biological protection, it identifies hypothesis-generating biomarkers that warrant validation in independent prospective cohorts and supports the potential value of comprehensive serological profiling for future cancer risk stratification.

title: Bronquiolitis en pediatría: diagnóstico clínico y manejo actualizado basado en evidencia
abstract: Bronchiolitis is the main lower respiratory tract infection in infants and a frequent cause of paediatric hospitalisation during epidemic seasons. The study therefore aimed to analyse the scientific evidence on the diagnosis and updated management of bronchiolitis in children under two years of age. A qualitative systematic review was conducted in PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane and Scopus, with a sample of 24 studies published between 2020 and 2025, selected from 124 records. Respiratory syncytial virus was the predominant agent, diagnosis was clinical, supportive care with hydration, nasal suction and oxygen for hypoxaemia was the basis of management, and bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics showed no routine benefit. It was concluded that high-flow nasal cannula and passive or maternal immunisation strengthen the current approach.

title: Deep untargeted wastewater metagenomic sequencing from sewersheds across the United States
abstract: Wastewater monitoring enables non-invasive, population-scale tracking of community infections independent of healthcare-seeking behavior and clinical diagnosis. Metagenomic sequencing extends this capability by enabling broad, pathogen-agnostic detection of hundreds of viral taxa, including emerging threats. Here, we present data from CASPER (the Coalition for Agnostic Sequencing of Pathogens from Environmental Reservoirs), a U.S.-based wastewater metagenomic sequencing network designed for deep, untargeted pathogen monitoring at national scale. This release includes 1,206 samples collected between December 2023 and December 2025 from 27 sites across nine states, covering 13 million people. Deep sequencing (~1 billion read pairs per sample) generated 1.2 trillion read pairs (358 terabases), capturing diverse human, animal, and plant viruses including rare taxa. CASPER data tracks wastewater digital PCR and clinical abundance trends for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and respiratory syncytial virus, and recovers national-scale variant dynamics for SARS-CoV-2 and norovirus. As the largest publicly available untargeted wastewater sequencing dataset to date, CASPER provides a shared and growing resource for pathogen surveillance and microbial ecology.

full_text: Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis, or scrofula, may be the first manifestation of previously undiagnosed advanced HIV, even when concurrent miliary pulmonary tuberculosis produces few or no respiratory symptoms. A 25-year-old male immigrant from Eastern Europe presented with one to two weeks of progressive right cervical and jaw swelling, fever, night sweats, fatigue, and anorexia, without cough, dyspnea, or chest pain. Neck and chest computed tomography demonstrated necrotic bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, supraclavicular and paratracheal adenopathy, and diffuse miliary pulmonary nodularity. HIV testing revealed advanced untreated infection with a CD4 count of 174 cells/mm3 and HIV-1 RNA of 956,000 copies/mL; QuantiFERON-TB Gold (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) was positive. Cervical lymph node biopsy demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli. Because the patient could not produce sputum, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed, and BAL Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) polymerase chain reaction detected MTB complex with rifampin resistance not detected. He was started on rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol therapy with pyridoxine and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine and dolutegravir was initiated six weeks after antituberculous therapy. Two weeks after ART initiation, he developed recurrent neck swelling and fever with new contralateral cervical lymphadenopathy, while HIV-1 RNA had declined to 2,180 copies/mL and CD4 count had risen to 190 cells/mm3. After consideration of treatment failure, drug resistance, bacterial infection, other opportunistic infection, and malignancy, the presentation was felt to be most consistent with paradoxical tuberculosis-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS). Symptoms improved with conservative management and close monitoring. He completed the 60-day intensive phase of antituberculous therapy, transitioned to rifampin and isoniazid continuation therapy, and remained on ART. This case highlights that cervical scrofula may reveal advanced, previously undiagnosed HIV with radiographically extensive but clinically silent miliary tuberculosis, and that recurrent lymphadenopathy after ART initiation should prompt consideration of paradoxical TB-IRIS while alternative diagnoses are evaluated. DiscussionThis case illustrates the radiographic-clinical discordance characteristic of TB in advanced HIV. With CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm3, impaired granuloma formation can yield atypical presentations, including miliary patterns and lymphadenopathy rather than classic cavitary disease [3,4]. Patients with low CD4 counts show more lymphadenopathy and miliary patterns but less cavitation than those with higher CD4 counts [3]. Sputum smear microscopy has poor sensitivity in people with HIV, and many hospitalized patients with HIV infection are unable to produce sputum samples [4,5]. Absent respiratory symptoms despite extensive imaging findings may reflect blunted immune-mediated inflammation. Subclinical TB, defined by positive cultures without symptoms, has been reported among people with untreated HIV [4]. Scrofula remains an under-appreciated manifestation of extrapulmonary TB in undiagnosed HIV, and lymph node involvement is common in HIV-related TB [6,7].This patient carried significant risk for IRIS given his CD4 count, high viral load, and extrapulmonary disease. A meta-analysis reported a pooled paradoxical TB-IRIS incidence of 18% among adults with HIV-associated TB initiating ART, with death attributed to TB-IRIS in 2% of cases [4,8]. Consistently identified risk factors include low CD4 count, high HIV viral load, disseminated or extrapulmonary TB, and a short interval between starting TB treatment and initiating ART [7,9,10]. Common manifestations of paradoxical TB-IRIS include recurrent respiratory symptoms with worsening pulmonary infiltrates and enlarged lymph nodes, which may form pus, resembling this patient's disease pattern [4]. DHHS guidelines recommend ART initiation in HIV-associated TB based on CD4 count, TB site, disease severity, and IRIS risk. For ART-naïve patients with CD4 counts >50 cells/mm3 and no suspected CNS or tuberculous meningitis involvement, ART is generally initiated within two to eight weeks after starting antituberculous therapy [7,11,12]. In this case, ART was initiated six weeks after antituberculous therapy given the patient’s CD4 count of 174 cells/mm3, absence of suspected CNS involvement, disseminated disease, and concern for IRIS risk. ConclusionsThis case highlights several practical considerations for clinicians. In immunocompromised patients with unexplained cervical lymphadenopathy, particularly when nodes are necrotic, TB should be considered even in the absence of cough or other respiratory symptoms. HIV testing and chest imaging should be considered when TB is suspected. When sputum cannot be obtained, lymph node sampling for histopathology and mycobacterial testing may aid diagnosis, with bronchoscopy considered when additional pulmonary microbiologic confirmation is needed. After ART initiation, new or recurrent fever and lymphadenopathy should prompt evaluation for paradoxical TB-IRIS while also assessing for treatment failure, drug resistance, bacterial or opportunistic infection, and malignancy. Early recognition of these patterns may help reduce diagnostic delay and facilitate coordinated treatment of TB and HIV. IntroductionTuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of death among people with HIV, and extrapulmonary disease becomes increasingly common as immunosuppression progresses, occurring in roughly 70% of patients with CD4 counts ≤100 cells/mm3 compared with about 30% of those with counts >300 cells/mm3 [1]. Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis is among the most common extrapulmonary manifestations of TB in people with HIV [2]. Although disseminated TB is well recognized in advanced HIV, less attention has been given to presentations in which striking miliary pulmonary involvement is accompanied by minimal or absent respiratory symptoms and cervical lymphadenopathy serves as the first clinical clue to previously undiagnosed HIV. This radiographic-clinical discordance may delay recognition if clinicians rely on pulmonary symptoms to raise suspicion for TB. We report this case to highlight cervical scrofula as a sentinel presentation of advanced, previously undiagnosed HIV with clinically silent miliary tuberculosis and to emphasize the subsequent risk of paradoxical TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS) following antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation. Case presentationA 25-year-old male immigrant from Eastern Europe with a history of asthma and chronic tonsillitis presented with one to two weeks of progressive right-sided neck and jaw swelling, fever, chills, night sweats, fatigue, and decreased appetite. He denied dyspnea, productive cough, or chest pain. Initial differentials included odontogenic infection, parotitis, sialadenitis, and lymphoma. CT of the chest demonstrated innumerable, diffuse, bilateral, randomly distributed pulmonary micronodules consistent with a miliary pattern, raising concern for disseminated TB (Figure 1). CT of the neck with contrast revealed extensive bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy with cystic and necrotic nodes, greater on the right, as well as supraclavicular and paratracheal adenopathy, consistent with cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis (Figure 2).Figure 1Miliary Pulmonary TuberculosisCT chest demonstrating diffuse bilateral randomly distributed pulmonary micronodules consistent with a miliary pattern, with representative nodules indicated by arrows.Figure 2Cervical Tuberculous Lymphadenitis (Scrofula)Coronal contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrating extensive bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, greater on the right, with central low attenuation consistent with necrotic cervical lymph nodes and cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis/scrofula. Arrows indicate representative necrotic nodes.Laboratory findings revealed lymphopenia and mild hyponatremia. HIV diagnostic testing was positive by fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody screening, with confirmatory testing consistent with HIV-1 infection. Baseline immune and virologic evaluation demonstrated a CD4 count of 174 cells/mm3 and an HIV-1 RNA level of 956,000 copies/mL, consistent with advanced untreated HIV infection. QuantiFERON-TB Gold (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) was positive. Despite extensive radiographic disease, the patient maintained normal oxygen saturation on room air and was unable to produce spontaneous sputum. Interventional radiology-guided core biopsy of a right cervical lymph node was performed to evaluate the necrotic cervical lymphadenopathy. Because a sputum specimen was not available for microbiologic testing, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) of the right upper lobe was pursued for confirmation. ART was intentionally deferred, with plans to initiate within two to eight weeks per Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) guidelines for patients with CD4 counts ≥50 cells/mm3 [1,2]. ART, consisting of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine and dolutegravir, was initiated six weeks after starting antituberculous therapy, in accordance with DHHS guidelines [1,2]. Because the patient was receiving rifampin-containing antituberculous therapy, dolutegravir was dosed at 50 mg twice daily during rifampin coadministration, consistent with guideline-based recommendations. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis was discontinued after a resolving drug rash, and prophylaxis was changed to dapsone 100 mg daily. HIV-1 RNA had declined to 2,180 copies/mL and CD4 count had risen to 190 cells/mm3, supporting immune recovery after ART initiation. Given the patient’s recurrent lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms after ART initiation, the differential diagnosis included paradoxical TB-IRIS, TB treatment failure, drug-resistant TB, bacterial lymphadenitis or superinfection, other opportunistic infections, and malignancy. Malignancy was considered less likely given the initial lymph node biopsy findings, which showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without evidence of malignancy. Treatment failure and drug-resistant TB were also considered; however, the patient had prior diagnostic confirmation of TB, was receiving antituberculous therapy, and BAL MTB PCR had shown rifampin resistance not detected. No alternative bacterial or opportunistic infection was identified in the available records. Given the temporal association with ART initiation and the absence of documented evidence supporting these alternative diagnoses, the presentation was felt to be most consistent with a paradoxical TB-IRIS-related inflammatory process. Symptoms were managed conservatively with close monitoring, with corticosteroids reserved should symptoms worsen. The intensive phase of RIPE therapy was completed after 60 days, and the patient transitioned to a four-month continuation phase of rifampin and isoniazid, while ART and antituberculous therapy were continued.

After consideration of treatment failure, drug resistance, bacterial infection, other opportunistic infection, and malignancy, the presentation was felt to be most consistent with paradoxical tuberculosis-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS). Symptoms improved with conservative management and close monitoring. He completed the 60-day intensive phase of antituberculous therapy, transitioned to rifampin and isoniazid continuation therapy, and remained on ART. This case highlights that cervical scrofula may reveal advanced, previously undiagnosed HIV with radiographically extensive but clinically silent miliary tuberculosis, and that recurrent lymphadenopathy after ART initiation should prompt consideration of paradoxical TB-IRIS while alternative diagnoses are evaluated.
full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis case illustrates the radiographic-clinical discordance characteristic of TB in advanced HIV. With CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm3, impaired granuloma formation can yield atypical presentations, including miliary patterns and lymphadenopathy rather than classic cavitary disease [3,4]. Patients with low CD4 counts show more lymphadenopathy and miliary patterns but less cavitation than those with higher CD4 counts [3]. Sputum smear microscopy has poor sensitivity in people with HIV, and many hospitalized patients with HIV infection are unable to produce sputum samples [4,5]. Absent respiratory symptoms despite extensive imaging findings may reflect blunted immune-mediated inflammation. Subclinical TB, defined by positive cultures without symptoms, has been reported among people with untreated HIV [4]. Scrofula remains an under-appreciated manifestation of extrapulmonary TB in undiagnosed HIV, and lymph node involvement is common in HIV-related TB [6,7].This patient carried significant risk for IRIS given his CD4 count, high viral load, and extrapulmonary disease. A meta-analysis reported a pooled paradoxical TB-IRIS incidence of 18% among adults with HIV-associated TB initiating ART, with death attributed to TB-IRIS in 2% of cases [4,8]. Consistently identified risk factors include low CD4 count, high HIV viral load, disseminated or extrapulmonary TB, and a short interval between starting TB treatment and initiating ART [7,9,10]. Common manifestations of paradoxical TB-IRIS include recurrent respiratory symptoms with worsening pulmonary infiltrates and enlarged lymph nodes, which may form pus, resembling this patient's disease pattern [4]. DHHS guidelines recommend ART initiation in HIV-associated TB based on CD4 count, TB site, disease severity, and IRIS risk. For ART-naïve patients with CD4 counts >50 cells/mm3 and no suspected CNS or tuberculous meningitis involvement, ART is generally initiated within two to eight weeks after starting antituberculous therapy [7,11,12]. In this case, ART was initiated six weeks after antituberculous therapy given the patient’s CD4 count of 174 cells/mm3, absence of suspected CNS involvement, disseminated disease, and concern for IRIS risk.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsThis case highlights several practical considerations for clinicians. In immunocompromised patients with unexplained cervical lymphadenopathy, particularly when nodes are necrotic, TB should be considered even in the absence of cough or other respiratory symptoms. HIV testing and chest imaging should be considered when TB is suspected. When sputum cannot be obtained, lymph node sampling for histopathology and mycobacterial testing may aid diagnosis, with bronchoscopy considered when additional pulmonary microbiologic confirmation is needed. After ART initiation, new or recurrent fever and lymphadenopathy should prompt evaluation for paradoxical TB-IRIS while also assessing for treatment failure, drug resistance, bacterial or opportunistic infection, and malignancy. Early recognition of these patterns may help reduce diagnostic delay and facilitate coordinated treatment of TB and HIV.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionTuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of death among people with HIV, and extrapulmonary disease becomes increasingly common as immunosuppression progresses, occurring in roughly 70% of patients with CD4 counts ≤100 cells/mm3 compared with about 30% of those with counts >300 cells/mm3 [1]. Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis is among the most common extrapulmonary manifestations of TB in people with HIV [2]. Although disseminated TB is well recognized in advanced HIV, less attention has been given to presentations in which striking miliary pulmonary involvement is accompanied by minimal or absent respiratory symptoms and cervical lymphadenopathy serves as the first clinical clue to previously undiagnosed HIV. This radiographic-clinical discordance may delay recognition if clinicians rely on pulmonary symptoms to raise suspicion for TB. We report this case to highlight cervical scrofula as a sentinel presentation of advanced, previously undiagnosed HIV with clinically silent miliary tuberculosis and to emphasize the subsequent risk of paradoxical TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS) following antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation. Case presentationA 25-year-old male immigrant from Eastern Europe with a history of asthma and chronic tonsillitis presented with one to two weeks of progressive right-sided neck and jaw swelling, fever, chills, night sweats, fatigue, and decreased appetite. Arrows indicate representative necrotic nodes.Laboratory findings revealed lymphopenia and mild hyponatremia. full_text: AbstractBackground: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) remain a major cause of hospitalization and mortality, particularly among children and other vulnerable populations. Early identification of pathogens and disease severity is essential for clinical decision-making. This study evaluated the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI and the prognostic utility of the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score) in a predominantly pediatric cohort.Methods: In this retrospective study, 117 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative SARI patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted to a tertiary care hospital in North India between September and December 2021 were evaluated. Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B predominating. Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%), predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024).The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults.Sampling technique and patient selectionConsecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults.Pathogen detection and laboratory methodsRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA.Multiplex PCR for Respiratory PathogensRespiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls.Conventional Microbiological CultureBlood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival. ResultsA total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance.Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCROut of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders.Figure 2Distribution of pathogen positivity by multiplex PCR in patient samplesHRSV A/B was the most frequently identified organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Rhinovirus.mPCR+: multiplex polymerase chain reaction positive for at least one pathogen; RSV A/B: respiratory syncytial virus types A and B; S. pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae; S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; HRV: human rhinovirus; IBV: influenza B virus; HPIV-4: human parainfluenza virus type 4; HAdV: human adenovirus; HCoV-OC43: human coronavirus OC43; HMPV A/B: human metapneumovirus types A and B; HPIV-3: human parainfluenza virus type 3; HPeV: human parechovirus; NPD: no pathogen detected; ARDS: acute respiratory distress syndrome; HD: hematological disordersPathogen detection profile from conventional culturesBlood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.Biomarker profileElevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis.ViVI Score distributionThe median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of median ViVI Scores across respiratory pathogens and coinfectionsThe table summarizes the median ViVI score with the corresponding interquartile range (IQR) for each identified organism or organism combination, along with the number of affected patients and classification as single infection or coinfection. ViVI scores reflect clinical severity at presentation, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity. Coinfections include viral-viral and viral-bacterial combinations detected by multiplex PCR and/or standard microbiological methods.HRSV: human respiratory syncytial virus; PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ViVI Score: ViVI Disease Severity ScoreOrganism / CoinfectionMedian ViVI scoreIQR (interquartile range)Number of patientsType of infectionHuman respiratory syncytial viruses A/B20.513.538Single InfectionStaphylococcus aureus20195Single InfectionInfluenza B virus20.510.254Single InfectionStreptococcus pneumoniae296.53Single InfectionHuman rhinovirus3562Single InfectionHuman adenovirus3701Single InfectionHuman parainfluenza virus 44201Single InfectionHRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2113.7510CoinfectionHRSV + Human rhinovirus2043CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B virus32162CoinfectionHRSV + Staphylococcus aureus 2032CoinfectionAdenovirus + HRSV1601CoinfectionCoronavirus OC43 + HRSV1601CoinfectionMetapneumovirus + HRSV4501CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 3 + Parainfluenza virus 41101CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 4 + Parechovirus801CoinfectionRhinovirus + Staphylococcus aureus 2901CoinfectionInfluenza B virus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2901CoinfectionStaphylococcus aureus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 3501CoinfectionHRSV + Parainfluenza virus 41501CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B + Staphylococcus aureus 2701CoinfectionClinical outcomes and mortalityThe overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases.Predictive utility of the ViVI ScoreA total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3).Figure 3Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrating the predictive performance of the ViVI Disease Severity Score for mortalityThe ROC plot displays the relationship between the false positive fraction (FPF: 1 − specificity) on the x-axis and the true positive fraction (TPF: sensitivity) on the y-axis across decision thresholds. The blue curve with red markers represents the binormal ROC curve fitted using maximum-likelihood estimation (JROCFIT), while the grey envelopes depict the 95% confidence interval around the fitted curve. The empirical (nonparametric) ROC operating points are shown as black markers (with the green connection, where applicable). Overall discrimination was excellent (fitted AUC ≈ 0.946; empirical AUC ≈ 0.942), with the curve lying close to the upper-left corner, indicating high sensitivity at low false-positive rates.The ROC curve lies close to the upper-left corner, indicating excellent discriminatory performance of the ViVI Score for predicting mortality across a range of decision thresholds (Figure 3). Using the ViVI Score as a mortality predictor and classifying death as the event, a low cutoff of ViVI ≥15 yielded 100% sensitivity for death (24/24) but low specificity (29.0%, 27/93) (TP=24, FN=0, TN=27, FP=66). In contrast, a high cutoff of ViVI ≥45 yielded 100% specificity (93/93) but low sensitivity (25.0%, 6/24) (TP=6, FN=18, TN=93, FP=0). The optimal threshold by Youden's J was ViVI ≥30, which provided balanced performance (sensitivity 83.3% (20/24) and specificity 91.4% (85/93); overall accuracy 89.7% (105/117)) (TP=20, FN=4, TN=85, FP=8). Patients with ViVI ≥30 had markedly increased odds of death compared with those with ViVI <30 (odds ratio 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; Fisher's exact test p=1.4 × 10−12). DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B predominating. Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%), predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024).The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults.Sampling technique and patient selectionConsecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults.Pathogen detection and laboratory methodsRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA.Multiplex PCR for Respiratory PathogensRespiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls.Conventional Microbiological CultureBlood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival.
full_text_sections.results: ResultsA total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance.Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCROut of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders.Figure 2Distribution of pathogen positivity by multiplex PCR in patient samplesHRSV A/B was the most frequently identified organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Rhinovirus.mPCR+: multiplex polymerase chain reaction positive for at least one pathogen; RSV A/B: respiratory syncytial virus types A and B; S. pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae; S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; HRV: human rhinovirus; IBV: influenza B virus; HPIV-4: human parainfluenza virus type 4; HAdV: human adenovirus; HCoV-OC43: human coronavirus OC43; HMPV A/B: human metapneumovirus types A and B; HPIV-3: human parainfluenza virus type 3; HPeV: human parechovirus; NPD: no pathogen detected; ARDS: acute respiratory distress syndrome; HD: hematological disordersPathogen detection profile from conventional culturesBlood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.Biomarker profileElevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis.ViVI Score distributionThe median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of median ViVI Scores across respiratory pathogens and coinfectionsThe table summarizes the median ViVI score with the corresponding interquartile range (IQR) for each identified organism or organism combination, along with the number of affected patients and classification as single infection or coinfection. ViVI scores reflect clinical severity at presentation, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity. Coinfections include viral-viral and viral-bacterial combinations detected by multiplex PCR and/or standard microbiological methods.HRSV: human respiratory syncytial virus; PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ViVI Score: ViVI Disease Severity ScoreOrganism / CoinfectionMedian ViVI scoreIQR (interquartile range)Number of patientsType of infectionHuman respiratory syncytial viruses A/B20.513.538Single InfectionStaphylococcus aureus20195Single InfectionInfluenza B virus20.510.254Single InfectionStreptococcus pneumoniae296.53Single InfectionHuman rhinovirus3562Single InfectionHuman adenovirus3701Single InfectionHuman parainfluenza virus 44201Single InfectionHRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2113.7510CoinfectionHRSV + Human rhinovirus2043CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B virus32162CoinfectionHRSV + Staphylococcus aureus 2032CoinfectionAdenovirus + HRSV1601CoinfectionCoronavirus OC43 + HRSV1601CoinfectionMetapneumovirus + HRSV4501CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 3 + Parainfluenza virus 41101CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 4 + Parechovirus801CoinfectionRhinovirus + Staphylococcus aureus 2901CoinfectionInfluenza B virus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2901CoinfectionStaphylococcus aureus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 3501CoinfectionHRSV + Parainfluenza virus 41501CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B + Staphylococcus aureus 2701CoinfectionClinical outcomes and mortalityThe overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases.Predictive utility of the ViVI ScoreA total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3).Figure 3Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrating the predictive performance of the ViVI Disease Severity Score for mortalityThe ROC plot displays the relationship between the false positive fraction (FPF: 1 − specificity) on the x-axis and the true positive fraction (TPF: sensitivity) on the y-axis across decision thresholds. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. The global burden of HRSV is substantial. A systematic analysis estimated 33.0 million HRSV-associated acute lower respiratory infection episodes, 3.6 million hospital admissions, and 101,400 deaths among children younger than five years in 2019, with the majority of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries [19].The frequency of co-infections observed in our cohort is also consistent with previous pediatric SARI studies using multiplex molecular platforms. Lamrani Hanchi et al. reported pathogen detection in 72.5% of hospitalized children and co-infection in 23.3%, highlighting the ability of multiplex PCR to identify multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen [20]. Similarly, studies incorporating digital surveillance and virological characterization have emphasized the value of combining pathogen detection with standardized clinical information [21,22]. These findings support the use of syndromic molecular testing as an adjunct to conventional microbiological investigations in patients with severe respiratory disease. However, detection of a respiratory pathogen does not necessarily establish causality, particularly for respiratory viruses that may be detected during prolonged shedding or asymptomatic infection. Therefore, multiplex PCR results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, disease severity, and conventional microbiological results.The exceptionally high mortality observed among SARI patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) was substantially higher than the overall mortality in the cohort. This finding is consistent with pediatric intensive-care data demonstrating significant mortality among children with bloodstream-infection-associated severe sepsis [23]. The finding emphasizes the importance of early recognition of bacterial superinfection and sepsis among patients presenting with severe respiratory illness, particularly when clinical deterioration or evidence of systemic infection is present.HRSV-associated disease severity is influenced by age and underlying clinical conditions. Recent multicenter pediatric data have demonstrated increased risk of severe RSV disease among younger children, premature infants, and older children with pulmonary or neurological, neuromuscular, or developmental conditions [24]. In our cohort, children with underlying hematological disorders represented an important high-risk subgroup, and HRSV-associated ARDS was associated with severe clinical outcomes. These findings reinforce the importance of identifying underlying risk factors when assessing patients with HRSV-associated SARI.The ViVI Score provided a structured approach to clinical severity assessment. Previous work has emphasized the importance of standardized severity assessment for respiratory viral illness and SARI [5]. More recent severity scales have also been evaluated to support respiratory hospitalization surveillance and viral genomic surveillance [25]. In our cohort, a ViVI score of ≥30 demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with an AUC of 0.946. This finding supports the potential utility of standardized severity assessment for identifying patients at increased risk of poor outcomes. However, prospective validation in independent populations is required before this threshold can be considered for broader clinical implementation.Raised PCT and CRP concentrations were associated with culture-positive sepsis and adverse clinical outcomes in our cohort. Previous pediatric data have evaluated PCT and CRP as markers of sepsis, with PCT potentially providing useful information regarding bacterial infection and disease severity [26]. However, neither biomarker should be interpreted as a stand-alone diagnostic test. Their value is greatest when interpreted together with the clinical presentation, microbiological findings, and other laboratory parameters.The findings also have implications for respiratory disease surveillance and clinical triage. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment can provide information on both pathogen circulation and clinical severity [21,22,25]. Such an approach may be particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings, where molecular diagnostic capacity is concentrated at tertiary-care facilities, and timely referral of patients with severe disease remains important. In primary-care settings, recognition of clinical warning signs and timely referral remain essential, while tertiary-care molecular testing can provide additional etiological information.The post-pandemic period is particularly relevant for respiratory pathogen surveillance because changes in population immunity, non-pharmaceutical interventions, and patterns of viral circulation may influence the timing and intensity of respiratory virus activity [16]. Continued surveillance is therefore important for identifying changing epidemiological patterns, detecting populations at increased risk of severe disease, and informing healthcare preparedness.The predominance of HRSV in our cohort also highlights the importance of preventive strategies. Current approaches to prevention of severe RSV disease include maternal vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibody strategies, particularly for infants at greatest risk of severe disease [27]. Continued pathogen-specific surveillance will be important for evaluating the epidemiological impact of these interventions.The study has several strengths. It integrates multiplex molecular diagnostics with conventional microbiological culture, inflammatory biomarkers, and standardized severity assessment, allowing simultaneous evaluation of pathogen distribution, bacterial superinfection, disease severity, and mortality. The use of a standardized severity score also enabled quantitative assessment of the relationship between clinical severity and mortality.In this study, several limitations should nevertheless be considered. The retrospective single-center design and relatively small sample size limit generalizability. The cohort was predominantly pediatric (103 children and 14 adults), which reflects the population evaluated at our center during the study period. Consequently, the findings, particularly those related to pathogen distribution, disease severity, and mortality risk stratification, should be interpreted primarily in the context of pediatric SARI and may not be directly generalizable to adult SARI populations. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsHRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen identified among hospitalized patients with non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI. Multiplex molecular testing provided useful etiological information, while the ViVI Score demonstrated good discriminatory ability for mortality risk in this cohort. Further prospective studies in larger and more diverse populations are needed to validate these findings.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSevere acute respiratory infections (SARI) pose a significant global health challenge, causing substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines SARI as an acute respiratory illness with a history of fever or measured fever of ≥38°C and cough, with onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization [1]. However, this syndromic definition does not provide information regarding the underlying etiological agent or the individual risk of adverse outcomes. SARI may result from a wide range of viral and bacterial pathogens, and conventional diagnostic methods may not always provide a timely or comprehensive etiological diagnosis.Before the COVID-19 pandemic, SARI detection was largely syndromic, relying on clinical presentation and limited diagnostic capacity [2]. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for strengthening surveillance systems and pathogen identification. In India, surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases is supported through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, including laboratory-based and information technology-enabled surveillance [3].SARI constitutes a major cause of healthcare utilization and hospitalization and may require referral to secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, particularly among young children, older adults, and individuals with underlying comorbidities. Family physicians are often the first point of contact for patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and therefore play a pivotal role in early recognition of severe disease, timely referral, initiation of appropriate management, and implementation of infection prevention measures [1,2]. Accurate identification of respiratory pathogens and early risk stratification are essential to improve patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use [2].In low- and middle-income countries such as India, access to specialized diagnostic services remains limited at primary-care facilities, with sample transport and referral mechanisms used to improve access to diagnostic testing [4]. Consequently, evidence on the etiological profile of SARI and validated clinical severity assessment tools is highly relevant for strengthening referral pathways, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory disease surveillance. Such evidence can assist family physicians and primary care providers in identifying patients requiring urgent referral, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and optimizing utilization of healthcare resources [2,4].To standardize clinical assessment, various severity scoring systems have been introduced. One of the most widely recognized is the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score), developed by the Vienna Vaccine Safety Initiative. This 22-item composite score quantifies the clinical severity of influenza-like illnesses and SARI across diverse patient populations [5]. It includes indicators of both uncomplicated and complicated disease, providing a standardized framework for clinical decision-making, disease severity assessment, and epidemiological comparison.The advent of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platforms has markedly advanced the diagnostic approach to SARI by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and expediting clinical decision-making [6]. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment has the potential to improve clinical risk stratification while strengthening pathogen-specific surveillance and facilitating the integration of virological and clinical data for surveillance and public health applications [6,7].Despite advances in molecular diagnostics and standardized severity assessment, evidence integrating pathogen identification with clinical risk stratification in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI remains limited, particularly from resource-constrained settings. Addressing this gap may help strengthen clinical decision-making, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory infection surveillance across primary and tertiary healthcare settings.
