title_original: Molecular Etiology and Mortality Risk Stratification of Non-SARS-CoV-2 Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in a Predominantly Pediatric Cohort: A Retrospective Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify the etiological profile of pathogens responsible for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) other than SARS-CoV-2 in a predominantly pediatric cohort, addressing the need for better diagnostic tools in resource-limited settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in North India from September to December 2021, analyzing 117 patients admitted with SARI during the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.methods: Multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture were used to detect respiratory pathogens. The study cohort comprised 103 children and 14 adults. Pathogen detection was performed using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus assay, and statistical analysis was conducted using Fisher’s exact test.
analysis.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the predominant pathogen. A cutoff of ≥30 in the ViVI Score yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity, strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, and bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. The ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with a cutoff of ≥30 showing strong association.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the ViVI Score can be a useful tool for clinical triage and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings, and HRSV is a significant cause of severe respiratory illness in children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the small sample size, which may affect generalizability. The high mortality rate in patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) highlights the need for better diagnostic and treatment strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This study identified HRSV as the predominant respiratory pathogen in a cohort of 117 pediatric and adult patients with severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) in North India. The ViVI Score, with a cutoff of ≥30, showed strong association with mortality (OR 53.1, p<0.001), suggesting its utility in clinical triage and surveillance.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify the etiological profile of pathogens responsible for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) other than SARS-CoV-2 in a predominantly pediatric cohort, addressing the need for better diagnostic tools in resource-limited settings.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in North India from September to December 2021, analyzing 117 patients admitted with SARI during the COVID-19 pandemic.
elements_en.methods: Multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture were used to detect respiratory pathogens. The study cohort comprised 103 children and 14 adults. Pathogen detection was performed using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus assay, and statistical analysis was conducted using Fisher’s exact test.
elements_en.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the predominant pathogen. A cutoff of ≥30 in the ViVI Score yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity, strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, and bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. The ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with a cutoff of ≥30 showing strong association.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the ViVI Score can be a useful tool for clinical triage and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings, and HRSV is a significant cause of severe respiratory illness in children.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the small sample size, which may affect generalizability. The high mortality rate in patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) highlights the need for better diagnostic and treatment strategies.

title: Development and validation of a nomogram for stratifying severe Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia risk in children early

source_records.title: Development and validation of a nomogram for stratifying severe Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia risk in children early

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop and validate a clinically applicable diagnostic predictive model to facilitate early identification of severe Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (SMPP) within 24 h of admission.MethodsClinical data from children with MPP hospitalized from January 2023 to December 2023, were retrospectively collected as the training set. Patients were classified into general MPP (GMPP) or SMPP groups based on whether SMPP occurred within 24 h of admission. After comparing the differences in clinical data between the two groups at admission, multivariate logistic regression was used to identify risk indicators for SMPP and construct a diagnostic predictive model. A nomogram was developed to visualize the model. Subsequently, data from children with MPP hospitalized between January 2024 and December 2024 were collected to conduct temporal external validation of the model. The predictive performance of the model was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and clinical impact curves (CIC).ResultsIn total, 412 children with MPP were included, with 222 cases within the training set (119 SMPP, 53.60%) and 190 within the temporal external validation set (129 SMPP, 67.89%). Independent risk indicators for the occurrence of SMPP included the duration of fever before admission (OR = 2.019, 95% CI: 1.387–2.938), shortness of breath (OR = 111.599, 95% CI: 11.512–1,081.834), unresponsive to macrolide before admission (OR = 3.687, 95% CI: 1.529–8.892), interleukin-6 (IL-6) (OR = 1.052, 95% CI: 1.010–1.095), and pulmonary consolidation (OR = 31.634, 95% CI: 11.643–85.948) (all P < 0.05). The nomogram based on the five aforementioned variables demonstrated favorable discriminative performance, with areas under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.916 (95% CI: 0.880–0.951) within the training set, 0.907 (95% CI: 0.873–0.946) within the internal validation, and 0.817 (95% CI: 0.758–0.876) within the temporal external validation set. The calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test showed that the model had good calibration. Both the DCA and CIC demonstrated favorable clinical utility of the model.ConclusionThe model developed in this study provides valuable reference for early risk stratification of pediatric SMPP and timely, individualized clinical decision-making in children with MPP. However, extensive external validation is required. 2Methods2.1Study subjectsClinical data from children with MPP who were hospitalized in the Department of Pediatrics of the Second People's Hospital of Futian District, Shenzhen, between January and December 2023 were retrospectively collected to form the training cohort. Patients were classified into GMPP and SMPP based on whether SMPP occurred within 24 h of admission. Data from patients with GMPP and SMPP admitted to the same hospital between January and December 2024 were then gathered to create a temporal external-validation set. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for both the training set and temporal external validation set were the same. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Age was 1–14 years; (ii) Diagnosis of MPP was based on the Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (2023) (15). Children were diagnosed with MPP if they presented with: (a) symptoms encompassing fever, cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath; (b) abnormal findings on lung auscultation and/or chest imaging indicative of pneumonia; and (c) at least one of the following laboratory criteria: (d) Positive MP-DNA; (e) A single serum MP antibody titer ≥1:160 [particle agglutination (PA) method]; or (f) An increase of fourfold or more in the MP antibody titer in paired serum samples during the course of the disease; (iii) Duration of fever at admission was ≥24 and ≤120 h; (iv) Complete data on cases. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Severe respiratory or circulatory system diseases, kidney or liver diseases, connective tissue diseases, and other underlying diseases; (ii) Long-term utilization of systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs; (iii) Duration of fever was >120 h at admission or without a fever before admission; (iv) People who were allergic to azithromycin, erythromycin, and doxycycline; (v) Use of systemic steroids, human immunoglobulin, or other treatments before confirming progression to SMPP; (vi) Incomplete data on cases (people with >50% missing laboratory data or without x-ray or CT examination); (vii) Laboratory test or chest imaging examination >24 h of admission; (viii) Age was <1 year or >14 years. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second People's Hospital of Futian District, Shenzhen. As a retrospective study with anonymized data collection, informed consent was unnecessary. The number of patients initially assessed, the reasons for exclusion, and the final sample sizes for each set described above are visually presented in the flowchart (Figure 1).Figure 1Flow chart of the study process.Flowchart diagram illustrates patient selection, exclusion criteria, cohort division, and statistical steps for constructing and validating a nomogram for Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in children, culminating in ROC, calibration, DCA, and CIC curve evaluations.2.2Collection of clinical dataClinical data of the children were collected through the electronic medical record system, encompassing demographic information, history of allergic diseases, clinical manifestations, laboratory tests [White blood cell count (WBC), neutrophil count (N), lymphocyte count (L), neutrophil percentage (N%), lymphocyte percentage (L%), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), hemoglobin (Hb), platelet count (PLT), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), IL-6, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), creatine kinase (CK), creatine kinase isoenzyme (CK-MB), uric acid (UA), albumin (ALB)], D-D, ferritin, respiratory pathogens (Influenza A Virus, Influenza B Virus, Parainfluenza Virus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus, Adenovirus, MP) identified by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), data derived from chest imaging, treatment before and after admission, and outcomes of patients. Clinical manifestations were derived from records during the initial course of the disease. Relevant laboratory and imaging indicators were obtained from tests conducted within 24 h of admission. If laboratory or imaging results were missing at admission, relevant test results obtained from outpatient examinations at the same hospital within 48 h prior to admission were used as substitutes.2.3Grouping schemeBased on the Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (2023) (15) and the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Children (2019 version) (18), children with MPP were classified into the SMPP group if they both met any of the following criteria within 24 h of admission and received additional corticosteroid therapy during hospitalization: (i) Persistent high fever (≥39 °C) for ≥5 days or ultra-hyperpyrexia; (ii) Shortness of breath and signs of increased work of breathing (moaning, nasal flaring, and suprasternal/intercostal/subcostal retractions); (iii) Presence of extrapulmonary complications; (iv) Oxygen saturation ≤93% without oxygen supplementation; (v) Chest imaging findings showing ≥2/3 consolidation of one lung or multi-lobar consolidation or the presence of pleural effusion; (vi) Progressive clinical symptoms with radiographic evidence of lesion progression, defined as a >50% increase in lesion size within 24–48 h. Patients who did not meet these criteria were included in the GMPP group.2.4Definition and assessment of variablesShortness of breath was defined as a respiratory rate ≥40 breaths per minute in children aged 1–5 years and ≥30 breaths per minute in children aged >5 years (18). Unresponsive to macrolide was defined as no clinical or radiological improvement or further deterioration after 48–72 h of macrolide treatment in MPP cases (15, 19). Pulmonary consolidation was defined as homogeneous dense opacity in at least one lobe, with or without an air-bronchogram in the lesion (20).2.5Data preprocessingFirst, patients were excluded if more than 50% of their laboratory test results were missing or if they lacked x-ray or CT examination results. Variables with >25% missing data were excluded, and multiple imputation was performed for all remaining covariates prior to statistical analysis to enhance methodological rigor and reduce potential selection bias. In the final dataset, we identified 11 variables from clinical manifestations, 9 variables from routine blood tests, 10 variables from biochemical detection data, 1 variable from respiratory pathogen tests, and 4 variables from imaging features.2.6Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were conducted using R (version 4.4.3). A two-tailed P < 0.05 signified statistical significance. Categorical variables were described using percentages (%), and inter-group comparisons were conducted using the Chi-square test. Normally distributed continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation, and inter-group comparisons were conducted using independent samples t-test. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were presented using the median and interquartile range (IQR), and inter-group comparisons were conducted using the Mann–Whitney U test. The variable differences were compared between the SMPP and GMPP groups in the training set. Variables with P < 0.1 were included in a multivariate logistic regression analysis to identify independent risk factors for SMPP. During this analysis, we used a probability threshold of 0.1 for exclusion and 0.05 for inclusion. Variance inflation factors (VIF) were used to analyze potential multicollinearity among the risk factors, and variables with a VIF >5 were excluded. A diagnostic predictive model that incorporated independent risk factors was constructed using logistic regression and then converted into a nomogram using the rms package. During the analysis, all continuous variables retained their original form and were not converted into categorical variables. Internal validation was performed using bootstrapping with 1,000 resamples. Clinical data from children with MPP admitted during a different time period from that of the training set were collected for temporal external validation of the model. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was plotted to estimate the discriminative capability of the model. The calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test were used to evaluate the prediction accuracy. Decision curve analysis (DCA) and clinical impact curve (CIC) were used to assess the clinical utility of the model (Figure 1). 3Results3.1Basic characteristics of included casesIn total, 412 children were included. The median age was 6 years (IQR 4.6–8.0), and 224 (54%) were boys. The median hospital days were 6 (IQR: 5–7). Among them, the training set included 222 cases (103 within the GMPP group and 119 within the SMPP group) and the temporal external validation set included 190 cases (61 within the GMPP group and 129 within the SMPP group). Significant differences between the training set and temporal external validation set were observed regarding the duration from fever to the first receipt of macrolides, WBC, N, L, PLT, PCT, IL-6 and ALT (P < 0.05) (Table 1). The roles of the training and validation sets and the process of model development and validation are shown in the flowchart (Figure 1). During the data analysis, data on D-D and ferritin were excluded because these tests were not performed in more than 25% of the included children. Routine blood test data for 31 children (7.5% of the total cohort) and chest imaging data for 86 children (18.4% of the total cohort) were obtained from outpatient examinations conducted within 48 h before admission. full_text_sections.abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop and validate a clinically applicable diagnostic predictive model to facilitate early identification of severe Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (SMPP) within 24 h of admission.MethodsClinical data from children with MPP hospitalized from January 2023 to December 2023, were retrospectively collected as the training set. Patients were classified into general MPP (GMPP) or SMPP groups based on whether SMPP occurred within 24 h of admission. After comparing the differences in clinical data between the two groups at admission, multivariate logistic regression was used to identify risk indicators for SMPP and construct a diagnostic predictive model. A nomogram was developed to visualize the model. Subsequently, data from children with MPP hospitalized between January 2024 and December 2024 were collected to conduct temporal external validation of the model. The predictive performance of the model was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and clinical impact curves (CIC).ResultsIn total, 412 children with MPP were included, with 222 cases within the training set (119 SMPP, 53.60%) and 190 within the temporal external validation set (129 SMPP, 67.89%). Independent risk indicators for the occurrence of SMPP included the duration of fever before admission (OR = 2.019, 95% CI: 1.387–2.938), shortness of breath (OR = 111.599, 95% CI: 11.512–1,081.834), unresponsive to macrolide before admission (OR = 3.687, 95% CI: 1.529–8.892), interleukin-6 (IL-6) (OR = 1.052, 95% CI: 1.010–1.095), and pulmonary consolidation (OR = 31.634, 95% CI: 11.643–85.948) (all P < 0.05). The nomogram based on the five aforementioned variables demonstrated favorable discriminative performance, with areas under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.916 (95% CI: 0.880–0.951) within the training set, 0.907 (95% CI: 0.873–0.946) within the internal validation, and 0.817 (95% CI: 0.758–0.876) within the temporal external validation set. The calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test showed that the model had good calibration. Both the DCA and CIC demonstrated favorable clinical utility of the model.ConclusionThe model developed in this study provides valuable reference for early risk stratification of pediatric SMPP and timely, individualized clinical decision-making in children with MPP. However, extensive external validation is required.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Methods2.1Study subjectsClinical data from children with MPP who were hospitalized in the Department of Pediatrics of the Second People's Hospital of Futian District, Shenzhen, between January and December 2023 were retrospectively collected to form the training cohort. Patients were classified into GMPP and SMPP based on whether SMPP occurred within 24 h of admission. Data from patients with GMPP and SMPP admitted to the same hospital between January and December 2024 were then gathered to create a temporal external-validation set. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for both the training set and temporal external validation set were the same. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Age was 1–14 years; (ii) Diagnosis of MPP was based on the Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (2023) (15). Children were diagnosed with MPP if they presented with: (a) symptoms encompassing fever, cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath; (b) abnormal findings on lung auscultation and/or chest imaging indicative of pneumonia; and (c) at least one of the following laboratory criteria: (d) Positive MP-DNA; (e) A single serum MP antibody titer ≥1:160 [particle agglutination (PA) method]; or (f) An increase of fourfold or more in the MP antibody titer in paired serum samples during the course of the disease; (iii) Duration of fever at admission was ≥24 and ≤120 h; (iv) Complete data on cases. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Severe respiratory or circulatory system diseases, kidney or liver diseases, connective tissue diseases, and other underlying diseases; (ii) Long-term utilization of systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs; (iii) Duration of fever was >120 h at admission or without a fever before admission; (iv) People who were allergic to azithromycin, erythromycin, and doxycycline; (v) Use of systemic steroids, human immunoglobulin, or other treatments before confirming progression to SMPP; (vi) Incomplete data on cases (people with >50% missing laboratory data or without x-ray or CT examination); (vii) Laboratory test or chest imaging examination >24 h of admission; (viii) Age was <1 year or >14 years. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second People's Hospital of Futian District, Shenzhen. As a retrospective study with anonymized data collection, informed consent was unnecessary. The number of patients initially assessed, the reasons for exclusion, and the final sample sizes for each set described above are visually presented in the flowchart (Figure 1).Figure 1Flow chart of the study process.Flowchart diagram illustrates patient selection, exclusion criteria, cohort division, and statistical steps for constructing and validating a nomogram for Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in children, culminating in ROC, calibration, DCA, and CIC curve evaluations.2.2Collection of clinical dataClinical data of the children were collected through the electronic medical record system, encompassing demographic information, history of allergic diseases, clinical manifestations, laboratory tests [White blood cell count (WBC), neutrophil count (N), lymphocyte count (L), neutrophil percentage (N%), lymphocyte percentage (L%), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), hemoglobin (Hb), platelet count (PLT), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), IL-6, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), creatine kinase (CK), creatine kinase isoenzyme (CK-MB), uric acid (UA), albumin (ALB)], D-D, ferritin, respiratory pathogens (Influenza A Virus, Influenza B Virus, Parainfluenza Virus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus, Adenovirus, MP) identified by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), data derived from chest imaging, treatment before and after admission, and outcomes of patients. Clinical manifestations were derived from records during the initial course of the disease. Relevant laboratory and imaging indicators were obtained from tests conducted within 24 h of admission. If laboratory or imaging results were missing at admission, relevant test results obtained from outpatient examinations at the same hospital within 48 h prior to admission were used as substitutes.2.3Grouping schemeBased on the Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (2023) (15) and the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Children (2019 version) (18), children with MPP were classified into the SMPP group if they both met any of the following criteria within 24 h of admission and received additional corticosteroid therapy during hospitalization: (i) Persistent high fever (≥39 °C) for ≥5 days or ultra-hyperpyrexia; (ii) Shortness of breath and signs of increased work of breathing (moaning, nasal flaring, and suprasternal/intercostal/subcostal retractions); (iii) Presence of extrapulmonary complications; (iv) Oxygen saturation ≤93% without oxygen supplementation; (v) Chest imaging findings showing ≥2/3 consolidation of one lung or multi-lobar consolidation or the presence of pleural effusion; (vi) Progressive clinical symptoms with radiographic evidence of lesion progression, defined as a >50% increase in lesion size within 24–48 h. Patients who did not meet these criteria were included in the GMPP group.2.4Definition and assessment of variablesShortness of breath was defined as a respiratory rate ≥40 breaths per minute in children aged 1–5 years and ≥30 breaths per minute in children aged >5 years (18). Unresponsive to macrolide was defined as no clinical or radiological improvement or further deterioration after 48–72 h of macrolide treatment in MPP cases (15, 19). Pulmonary consolidation was defined as homogeneous dense opacity in at least one lobe, with or without an air-bronchogram in the lesion (20).2.5Data preprocessingFirst, patients were excluded if more than 50% of their laboratory test results were missing or if they lacked x-ray or CT examination results. Variables with >25% missing data were excluded, and multiple imputation was performed for all remaining covariates prior to statistical analysis to enhance methodological rigor and reduce potential selection bias. In the final dataset, we identified 11 variables from clinical manifestations, 9 variables from routine blood tests, 10 variables from biochemical detection data, 1 variable from respiratory pathogen tests, and 4 variables from imaging features.2.6Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were conducted using R (version 4.4.3). A two-tailed P < 0.05 signified statistical significance. Categorical variables were described using percentages (%), and inter-group comparisons were conducted using the Chi-square test. Normally distributed continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation, and inter-group comparisons were conducted using independent samples t-test. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were presented using the median and interquartile range (IQR), and inter-group comparisons were conducted using the Mann–Whitney U test. The variable differences were compared between the SMPP and GMPP groups in the training set. Variables with P < 0.1 were included in a multivariate logistic regression analysis to identify independent risk factors for SMPP. During this analysis, we used a probability threshold of 0.1 for exclusion and 0.05 for inclusion. Variance inflation factors (VIF) were used to analyze potential multicollinearity among the risk factors, and variables with a VIF >5 were excluded. A diagnostic predictive model that incorporated independent risk factors was constructed using logistic regression and then converted into a nomogram using the rms package. During the analysis, all continuous variables retained their original form and were not converted into categorical variables. The median hospital days were 6 (IQR: 5–7). Among them, the training set included 222 cases (103 within the GMPP group and 119 within the SMPP group) and the temporal external validation set included 190 cases (61 within the GMPP group and 129 within the SMPP group). Significant differences between the training set and temporal external validation set were observed regarding the duration from fever to the first receipt of macrolides, WBC, N, L, PLT, PCT, IL-6 and ALT (P < 0.05) (Table 1). During the data analysis, data on D-D and ferritin were excluded because these tests were not performed in more than 25% of the included children. Routine blood test data for 31 children (7.5% of the total cohort) and chest imaging data for 86 children (18.4% of the total cohort) were obtained from outpatient examinations conducted within 48 h before admission. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionMPP is typically mild and self-limiting. Nevertheless, some children might progress to SMPP, which generally occurs around 1 week after the onset of symptoms. SMPP typically arises owing to failed early identification or delayed treatment beyond the optimal post-fever window within 5–7 days. Early recognition is fundamental for initiating effective therapy. These findings further underscore the critical need for timely diagnosis. Following the relaxation of non-pharmaceutical interventions in the post-COVID-19 era, a high global incidence of MP infections has emerged. In several countries (particularly China), reports have observed a considerable elevation in the clinical severity of MPP in children, with a rising proportion of SMPP cases (6–14). A study from Zurich, Switzerland, reported that, compared with the pre-COVID-19 period, children with MPP hospitalized between April 2022 and May 2024 exhibited significantly higher rates of chest pain, pleural effusion, and obstructive lung disease (5). A multicenter retrospective study conducted in Spain analyzed the clinical data of 542 children with MPP hospitalized from January 2023 to March 2024. That study revealed that 62% of children with MPP developed to SMPP after admission and required supplemental oxygen, while 14% were admitted to the pediatric intensive-care unit (7). A retrospective study from Romania categorized hospitalized children with MPP into two cohorts (2018–2019 and 2023–2024) and found that, compared to the pre-COVID-19 period, children with MPP in 2023–2024 experienced more severe progression of disease, with higher rates of pulmonary consolidation, gastrointestinal complications, and dyspnoea (21). Our study reviewed the clinical records of 420 children hospitalized for MPP in Shenzhen, China, during the 2023–2024 and observed that the proportion of SMPP cases reached 60.2%. This finding supports the observed trend toward more severe illness in Chinese children with MP infections after 2023. This shift in the epidemiology and clinical presentation of pediatric MPP indicates that delays in the diagnosis and treatment of SMPP must be addressed promptly. Given the high incidence of SMPP, pediatricians need to adopt updated diagnostic and therapeutic approaches in clinical practice. Furthermore, it is essential to heighten early vigilance for SMPP in children at an early stage. Following comprehensive assessment with validated scoring tools, personalized and precise treatment should be implemented based on the severity of disease to reduce the complications and mortality of SMPP in children. However, to date, no validated and widely used comprehensive predictive model that integrates clinical manifestations, laboratory indicators, and imaging characteristics has been established for pediatric SMPP. In this study, we developed and preliminarily validated a nomogram model incorporating five easily accessible variables. This model provides clinicians with a simple, clinically applicable visual tool for early diagnosis of SMPP in children within 24 h of admission.The early clinical symptoms of SMPP are non-specific and might progress rapidly. The Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (2023) (15) indicates that children with MPP who exhibit shortness of breath within the first 5 days of illness or persistent high fever ≥5 days, or fail to respond to 72-hour macrolide therapy from onset, should be considered at risk for SMPP. The results of our study support this perspective. This study showed a significantly higher proportion of shortness of breath in SMPP. The odds ratio (OR) was 111.599 (95% CI: 11.512–1,081.834), and the relative risk was higher relative to other four predictive factors. This finding suggests that shortness of breath might be the most valuable early clinical predictor of SMPP. However, previous study have shown that, shortness of breath demonstrates only 47% sensitivity for diagnosing SMPP (16). Combined with the findings of this study, shortness of breath as a single diagnostic indicator has a low sensitivity and a high specificity for diagnosing SMPP in children. Fever is a common clinical symptom of MPP. Prolonged fever can induce systemic immune dysfunction, compromising the management of infection and inflammation, triggering an excessive immune-inflammatory response, and thereby promoting the occurrence and progression of SMPP (22). Prior studies have compared the duration of fever among children with GMPP and SMPP and found that prolonged fever is a risk indicator for SMPP in children (10–13, 22). This study also observed that children in the SMPP group demonstrated prolonged fever periods before admission relative to the GMPP group, with a higher proportion of patients experiencing fever for 5 days before admission. Multivariate logistic regression further confirmed that the duration of fever before admission is an independent predictive factor for SMPP (OR = 2.019, 95% CI: 1.387–2.938, P < 0.05).Recently, emergence of macrolide-unresponsive MPP (MU-MPP) has complicated the management of MPP. MU-MPP is defined as MPP in which fever persists, and clinical signs and chest imaging show no improvement or further deterioration despite 48–72 h of macrolide therapy (15, 19). The primary cause of MU-MPP is the acquisition of resistance by MP through mutations in the 23S rRNA gene. Reduced susceptibility to macrolides leads to higher bacterial loads and a more intense immune-inflammatory response, resulting in more severe outcomes of diseases (10, 23). A study (23) in 2024 reported that, relative to children with macrolide-sensitive MPP, children with MU-MPP showed significantly prolonged duration of fever, a higher proportion of shortness of breath (23.61%) and hypoxemia (29.17%), and a higher proportion of progression to SMPP (52.78% vs. 34.83%; P < 0.05). This observation aligns with our findings. In our study, relative to the GMPP group, the SMPP group had an elevated proportion of unresponsive to macrolide before admission (61% vs. 44%, P < 0.05). The diagnosis of MU-MPP might serve as an early predictive indicator for SMPP (OR = 3.687, 95% CI: 1.529–8.892).After entering the bloodstream, MP stimulates immune cells, airway epithelium, and pulmonary fibroblasts to produce IL-6. Elevated levels of serum IL-6 are detectable among children with MPP early in the infection and induce an excessive immune-inflammatory response in the body, continuously invading the lungs and respiratory tissues, inducing poor amelioration of symptoms, and thereby exacerbating the disease (22). Several studies have shown that IL-6 can be used to estimate the severity of disease among children with MPP and serves as an early predictive marker for SMPP (22, 24). However, the optimal cutoff value of IL-6 for predicting SMPP remains underexplored. The results of this study indicate that an IL-6 level >8.625 ng/mL measured within 1–5 days of fever can facilitate early identification of SMPP in children with MPP.Chest imaging among children with MPP varies based on the severity of their condition. These manifestations might include bronchopneumonia, pulmonary consolidation, atelectasis, pleural effusion, and mosaic signs in the lungs. The severity of chest imaging findings is strongly linked to the clinical characteristics and outcomes of MPP. It might serve as an important indicator for prognosis (20, 25, 26). The study by Chu et al. (25) reported that low-dose chest CT has superior sensitivity and specificity relative to chest x-rays in diagnosing SMPP. Pulmonary consolidation is a stable and reliable CT feature, and quantitative analysis of lobar consolidation can comprehensively and accurately predict the progression of MPP in children. For suspected SMPP cases, low-dose chest CT may contribute to early identification. The study by Mu et al. (26) and Huang et al. showed that MPP children with pulmonary consolidation may develop complications su…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionIn conclusion, this study constructs a simple and intuitive early assessment nomogram-based model for SMPP in children, based on duration of fever before admission (days), shortness of breath, unresponsive to macrolide before admission, levels of IL-6, and pulmonary consolidation. Multidimensional performance evaluation and preliminary validation support the strong discriminative capability, excellent calibration, robust clinical utility, relatively good generalizability of the model in our center. The model enables clinicians to quantitatively estimate the probability of SMPP in children during the critical early febrile phase (days 1–5). This capability is potentially useful for early risk stratification of pediatric SMPP and may help fulfill the clinical objective of early diagnosis of SMPP within 24 h of admission. Future prospective multicenter clinical trials are required to validate its practical utility in clinical decision-making across diverse populations and medical centers. Once thoroughly externally validated, this nomogram model might serve as an auxiliary tool for clinicians to identify SMPP at an early stage, thereby facilitating individualized risk assessment, rapid clinical stratification, and precise treatment within 24 h of admission for children with MPP.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionMycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) is a major pathogen causing community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) among children. Globally, epidemics of Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MPP) occur every 3–7 years (1–4), accounting for >50% of pediatric hospitalizations for CAP during epidemic seasons. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, a global resurgence of MP infections emerged in 2023–2024. Reports from multiple countries [e.g., Germany (1), China (2, 3), Denmark (4), Switzerland (5), the UK (6), Spain (7), the USA (8), and other countries] indicate a significant rise in the incidence of pediatric MPP. Although MPP is typically mild and most children respond well to macrolide therapy, the incidence of severe MPP (SMPP) has risen recently (6–8), particularly in China (9–14). This trend may be attributable to rising prevalence of macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MRMP), heightened host immune-inflammatory responses, and increased co-infections. Various pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications caused by SMPP, such as plastic bronchitis, necrotizing pneumonia, and involvement of the neurological, circulatory, digestive, hematological, and mucocutaneous systems, might lead to life-threatening conditions and sequelae (15). These outcomes pose significant threats to health of children and increase healthcare burdens. Therefore, it is necessary to identify SMPP early and initiate effective treatment promptly. This might help children avoid or mitigate complications and sequelae, which is vital for improving prognosis.Because epidemiological characteristics, clinical practice needs, and healthcare resource allocation vary across countries and regions, no unified diagnostic criteria for SMPP in children have been established worldwide. The Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (15) proposes several diagnostic criteria for SMPP, including clinical manifestations (e.g., tachypnea, hypoxemia), abnormal chest imaging findings (e.g., x-ray or CT showing ≥2/3 consolidation of one lung or multi-lobar consolidation), and significant increases in inflammatory biomarkers [e.g., lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), D-dimer (D-D), C-reactive protein (CRP)]. The guideline states that cases are categorized as SMPP if patients meet any of the above criteria. However, these severity assessment criteria have not been systematically derived or clinically validated in the pediatric population. Previous studies suggest that the diagnostic performance of these individual markers is suboptimal (16, 17), and the optimal predictive thresholds for serological markers remain unclear. Furthermore, the clinical manifestations of SMPP in children are highly heterogeneous, and MPP can progress rapidly in children. Consequently, early identification of SMPP remains challenging. Owing to the absence of quantitative scoring for these risk indicators, it has been impossible to conduct individualized, precise quantification of the risk of SMPP in each child with MPP. Therefore, a quantitative scoring tool that can accurately and individually predict the risk of SMPP at an early stage needs to be developed. Recently, nomogram-based prediction models have been widely applied to assess the risk of pediatric diseases owing to their favorable predictive accuracy and simple, intuitive visualization (11–14). Nevertheless, nomograms specifically designed for the early diagnostic prediction of SMPP among children remain scarce. Moreover, the clinical utility and predictive performance of existing models have not been externally validated (11–13). Their generalizability is uncertain, and they are currently not suitable for dissemination as standardized assessment tools. This study aimed to investigate the clinical manifestations, laboratory indicators, and imaging characteristics of children with MPP in the early stages of the disease (within 1–5 days of fever), identify the independent risk indicators for the occurrence of SMPP, and integrate these multidimensional variables to construct a nomogram-based comprehensive model for early SMPP diagnosis within 24 h of admission. Moreover, the stability and generalizability of this model were assessed using internal validation and temporal external validation. These findings might provide a simple, rapid, and scientifically validated quantitative scoring tool for the early identification of SMPP among children and assist clinicians in detecting and treating SMPP during the critical early febrile phase (days 1–5), thereby reducing the occurrence of complications and sequelae. 2.1Study subjectsClinical data from children with MPP who were hospitalized in the Department of Pediatrics of the Second People's Hospital of Futian District, Shenzhen, between January and December 2023 were retrospectively collected to form the training cohort. Patients were classified into GMPP and SMPP based on whether SMPP occurred within 24 h of admission. Data from patients with GMPP and SMPP admitted to the same hospital between January and December 2024 were then gathered to create a temporal external-validation set. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for both the training set and temporal external validation set were the same. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Age was 1–14 years; (ii) Diagnosis of MPP was based on the Chinese Consensus Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of MPP in Children (2023) (15). Children were diagnosed with MPP if they presented with: (a) symptoms encompassing fever, cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath; (b) abnormal findings on lung auscultation and/or chest imaging indicative of pneumonia; and (c) at least one of the following laboratory criteria: (d) Positive MP-DNA; (e) A single serum MP antibody titer ≥1:160 [particle agglutination (PA) method]; or (f) An increase of fourfold or more in the MP antibody titer in paired serum samples during the course of the disease; (iii) Duration of fever at admission was ≥24 and ≤120 h; (iv) Complete data on cases. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Severe respiratory or circulatory system diseases, kidney or liver diseases, connective tissue diseases, and other underlying diseases; (ii) Long-term utilization of systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs; (iii) Duration of fever was >120 h at admission or without a fever before admission; (iv) People who were allergic to azithromycin, erythromycin, and doxycycline; (v) Use of systemic steroids, human immunoglobulin, or other treatments before confirming progression to SMPP; (vi) Incomplete data on cases (people with >50% missing laboratory data or without x-ray or CT examination); (vii) Laboratory test or chest imaging examination >24 h of admission; (viii) Age was <1 year or >14 years. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second People's Hospital of Futian District, Shenzhen. As a retrospective study with anonymized data collection, informed consent was unnecessary. The number of patients initially assessed, the reasons for exclusion, and the final sample sizes for each set described above are visually presented in the flowchart (Figure 1).Figure 1Flow chart of the study process.Flowchart diagram illustrates patient selection, exclusion criteria, cohort division, and statistical steps for constructing and validating a nomogram for Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in children, culminating in ROC, calibration, DCA, and CIC curve evaluations. 2.2Collection of clinical dataClinical data of the children were collected through the electronic medical record system, encompassing demographic information, history of allergic diseases, clinical manifestations, laboratory tests [White blood cell count (WBC), neutrophil count (N), lymphocyte count (L), neutrophil percentage (N%), lymphocyte percentage (L%), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), hemoglobin (Hb), platelet count (PLT), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), IL-6, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), alanine aminotransferase…

full_text: AbstractObjectivesTo analyze the epidemiological characteristics of six common respiratory pathogens in cases of Acute Respiratory Tract Infection (ARTI) in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025, to provide a basis for clinical diagnosis and treatment, as well as public health prevention and control.MethodsA multicenter retrospective study was conducted. Data from 81,974 ARTI cases from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou City between January 2018 and December 2025 were collected. Cases with positive test results were analyzed for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP), and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.ResultsAmong 81,974 patients, a total of 33,350 cases tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positive rate of 40.68%. MP (19.56%) and FluA (16.93%) were the most prevalent pathogens. The positivity rates of each pathogen showed statistically significant differences across the three stages before, during, and after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (all P < 0.001). Compared with the pre-COVID-19 pandemic period (2018–2019), the positive rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022), and then experienced a sharp “revenge rebound” in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025) (for example, the positive rate of MP rebounded from 5.43% to 21.09%). In contrast, the positive rates of RSV, ADV, and CP showed a persistent state of inhibition, but the absolute number of cases far exceeded that of before the COVID-19 pandemic. MP had the highest infection rate among 6– < 12 years old (38.31%), whereas FluA was more common in adults. The epidemiological distribution showed obvious seasonal heterogeneity: FluA/FluB/RSV were more prevalent in winter, MP was active in autumn, and ADV was more prevalent in summer. The co-infection rate was 7.22% (5,922 cases), and the most common combination was FluA + MP, accounting for 53.82% of all co-infections.ConclusionFrom 2018 to 2025, the pathogen spectrum of ARTI in Hangzhou was mainly composed of MP and FluA. The COVID-19 pandemic and related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) have had a profound and heterogeneous impact on the epidemic pattern of respiratory pathogens. FluA, FluB, and MP showed the characteristics of “suppression-retaliatory rebound.” In the post-COVID-19 pandemic era, the activity of pathogens has clear seasonal, age, and gender distribution patterns, and the rate of mixed infections is high. The research results suggest that a dynamic monitoring system needs to be established, and targeted prevention and control measures should be implemented for key individuals and pathogens during high-incidence seasons.Keywords: Acute Respiratory Tract Infection, epidemiological characteristics, Hangzhou, influenza virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, pathogen spectrum 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study populationThis study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens—influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), RSV, adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP)—among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, and to evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics. A total of 81,974 patients from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou seven medical institutions in Hangzhou (see Supplementary Table 1 for details) between January 2018 and December 2025 were selected as study subjects. The diagnostic criteria for cases were as follows: pediatric cases were defined according to the Practical Pediatrics (Zhu Futang, 8th edition) (8), while adult cases were defined according to the Expert consensus on the diagnosis, treatment, and infection control of acute respiratory infections in adult outpatient and emergency departments (9), including: (1) Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI): presence of ≥2 symptoms—fever (body temperature ≥38 °C), cough, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, or sneezing—with a duration of ≤ 7 days. (2) Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI): Clinical signs: increased respiratory rate, moist rales/whistling sounds in the lungs, or tracheal retractions; Radiological evidence (X-ray/CT): signs of pneumonia/bronchitis (e.g., patchy infiltrates, atelectasis). Exclusion criteria: Incomplete clinical data, incomplete pathogen detection results, or duplicate records. Clinical data from 1,431,696 individuals undergoing respiratory pathogen screening were collected in this study. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we excluded entries with incomplete pathogen detection, removed duplicate data from repeated hospitalizations and repeated outpatient visits (1,331,565 cases), as well as duplicate data between outpatient and inpatient records (18,157 cases). Ultimately, a total of 81,974 subjects were included in the statistical analysis (Figure 1).Figure 1Flowchart of the study.Flowchart illustrating a retrospective study design, showing data collection from seven medical institutions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, cohort selection process, analysis dimensions, and six key epidemiological outcomes for respiratory pathogen infections.2.2.Data collectionDemographic and clinical data of enrolled cases were collected through the “Xiaoshan Health Data Platform” platform. The determination of infection status was based on any of the following positive test results: positive serum pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, or positive pathogen antigens or nucleic acids detected in respiratory tract samples. This study encompasses six common respiratory pathogens, including FluA, FluB, RSV, ADV, MP, and CP. For all six pathogens, specimen types included nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swabs, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and blood; detection methods included serological IgM assays, antigen detection, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), with the exception that antigen detection was not included for CP. Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. Only patients with complete test results for all six target pathogens were included in the final analysis.Grouping of study subjects: in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for age-stage division and population age stratification, the study subjects were divided into six age groups: 0– < 3 years (infant and toddler group), 3– < 6 years (preschool group), 6– < 12 years (school-age group), 12– < 18 years (adolescence group), 18– < 60 years (adult group), and ≥60 years (older adult(s) group). According to year span, the subjects were divided into three periods: 2018–2019, 2020–2022, and 2023–2025. Seasonal grouping included spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), and winter (December–February of the following year). The chi-square (χ2) two-sided test was used for intergroup comparisons of qualitative data, and a P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.2.3.Statistical analysisData were exported to Excel, and statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.3.2. Normally distributed continuous data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, while non-normally distributed data are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR). Positivity rates for each study period were calculated as the total number of positive cases divided by the total number of tested cases across all years within that period. Count data are presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups were performed using the chi-square test. All tests were two-sided, and the significance level was set at α = 0.05. Calculation formula: Positive rate (%) = (Number of positive cases detected among the screened population / Total number of screened cases) × 100%. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1907370/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 3.Results3.1.Basic characteristics of the research subjectsAmong 81,974 patients with ARTI, 33,350 were positive for pathogens, with a positivity rate of 40.68%. Specifically, the positive rate for outpatient cases was 44.64% (30,405/68,109), and that for inpatient cases was 19.83% (2,749/13,865). Among the 81,974 ARTI patients screened from 2018 to 2025, the number of cases each year was 1,915, 3,116, 1,086, 1,676, 2,963, 19,630, 31,639, and 19,949, respectively. The pathogen positive rates were 21.78% (417/1,915), 26.03% (811/3,116), 14.09% (153/1,086), 10.80% (181/1,676), 14.21% (421/2,963), 51.08% (10,027/19,630), 39.03% (12,350/31,639), and 44.08% (8,794/19,949), respectively, as shown in Figure 2. There were 41,996 males and 39,978 females, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.05:1. The median age was 24.00 (5.00, 37.00) years.Figure 2The number and positive rate of respiratory pathogens in acute respiratory infection cases in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025.Stacked bar and line chart showing annual positive cases of a disease in outpatients and hospitalized patients from 2018 to 2025, with positive rates peaking in 2023 and 2024 before declining in 2025.Further stratified analysis revealed significant variations in the outpatient-inpatient positivity gap across subgroups (Supplementary Table 2). By age, the largest disparity was observed in children aged 3– < 6 years, with a positivity rate of 59.50% in outpatients compared to 22.44% in inpatients (difference of 36.9 percentage points). By time period, the gap widened markedly in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025: 51.27% vs. 22.93%) compared to the pre-COVID-19 pandemic period (2018–2019: 35.18% vs. 23.57%). By pathogen, Flu A, Flu B, and MP showed higher positivity in outpatients, whereas RSV, ADV, and CP were higher in inpatients.3.2.Analysis of the positive detection status of pathogens and their temporal trendsFrom 2018 to 2025, among the acute respiratory infection cases in Hangzhou, the detection results of six common respiratory pathogens showed that MP had the highest overall positive rate (19.56%, 16,035/81,974), followed by FluA (16.93%, 13,876/81,974). The overall positivity rates of the remaining four pathogens ranged from 0.23% to 7.25%, including FluB (7.25%, 5,946/81,974), RSV (2.45%, 2,007/81,974), ADV (1.85%, 1,518/81,974), and CP (0.23%, 190/81,974).Chi-square tests were performed to assess overall differences in the positive rates of each pathogen across the three period. The results indicated that the differences in the positive rates of each pathogen among the three periods were significant (all P < 0.001). Specifically, the positive rates of FluA, MP, and FluB showed a suppression during the COVID-19 pandemic period and rebounded significantly after the pandemic, presenting a typical “revenge-style epidemic” pattern, whereas, the positive rates of RSV, ADV, and CP showed a persistent state of inhibition, but the absolute number of cases was substantially higher than before the pandemic. The positive rates of MP and FluA from 2020 to 2022 demonstrated a decrease compared to 2018–2019 and from 2023 to 2025, showing an obvious “V-shaped” trend. Among them, the positive rate of MP during the COVID-19 pandemic period (5.43%) decreased by 61.1% compared with that before the pandemic (13.95%), and rebounded to 21.09% after the pandemic, an increase of 288.3% compared with the COVID-19 pandemic period; the positive rate of FluA during the COVID-19 pandemic period (1.57%) decreased by 58.5% compared with that before the pandemic (3.78%), and increased to 19.09% after the pandemic, an increase of 1115.9% compared with the COVID-19 pandemic period. The positive rates of ADV and CP from 2018 to 2019 were higher than those from 2020 to 2022 and from 2023 to 2025. The positive rate of ADV was 5.39% before the pandemic and decreased to 1.55% and 1.63% in the latter two periods, respectively; the positive rate of CP was 1.19% before the pandemic and decreased to 0.05% and 0.18% in the latter two periods, respectively. The positive rates of RSV were 3.08%, 2.90%, and 2.37% in the three periods, respectively, showing a gradual downward trend (P < 0.001). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectivesTo analyze the epidemiological characteristics of six common respiratory pathogens in cases of Acute Respiratory Tract Infection (ARTI) in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025, to provide a basis for clinical diagnosis and treatment, as well as public health prevention and control.MethodsA multicenter retrospective study was conducted. Data from 81,974 ARTI cases from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou City between January 2018 and December 2025 were collected. Cases with positive test results were analyzed for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP), and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.ResultsAmong 81,974 patients, a total of 33,350 cases tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positive rate of 40.68%. MP (19.56%) and FluA (16.93%) were the most prevalent pathogens. The positivity rates of each pathogen showed statistically significant differences across the three stages before, during, and after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (all P < 0.001). Compared with the pre-COVID-19 pandemic period (2018–2019), the positive rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022), and then experienced a sharp “revenge rebound” in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025) (for example, the positive rate of MP rebounded from 5.43% to 21.09%). In contrast, the positive rates of RSV, ADV, and CP showed a persistent state of inhibition, but the absolute number of cases far exceeded that of before the COVID-19 pandemic. MP had the highest infection rate among 6– < 12 years old (38.31%), whereas FluA was more common in adults. The epidemiological distribution showed obvious seasonal heterogeneity: FluA/FluB/RSV were more prevalent in winter, MP was active in autumn, and ADV was more prevalent in summer. The co-infection rate was 7.22% (5,922 cases), and the most common combination was FluA + MP, accounting for 53.82% of all co-infections.ConclusionFrom 2018 to 2025, the pathogen spectrum of ARTI in Hangzhou was mainly composed of MP and FluA. The COVID-19 pandemic and related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) have had a profound and heterogeneous impact on the epidemic pattern of respiratory pathogens. FluA, FluB, and MP showed the characteristics of “suppression-retaliatory rebound.” In the post-COVID-19 pandemic era, the activity of pathogens has clear seasonal, age, and gender distribution patterns, and the rate of mixed infections is high. The research results suggest that a dynamic monitoring system needs to be established, and targeted prevention and control measures should be implemented for key individuals and pathogens during high-incidence seasons.Keywords: Acute Respiratory Tract Infection, epidemiological characteristics, Hangzhou, influenza virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, pathogen spectrum
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study populationThis study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens—influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), RSV, adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP)—among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, and to evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics. A total of 81,974 patients from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou seven medical institutions in Hangzhou (see Supplementary Table 1 for details) between January 2018 and December 2025 were selected as study subjects. The diagnostic criteria for cases were as follows: pediatric cases were defined according to the Practical Pediatrics (Zhu Futang, 8th edition) (8), while adult cases were defined according to the Expert consensus on the diagnosis, treatment, and infection control of acute respiratory infections in adult outpatient and emergency departments (9), including: (1) Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI): presence of ≥2 symptoms—fever (body temperature ≥38 °C), cough, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, or sneezing—with a duration of ≤ 7 days. (2) Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI): Clinical signs: increased respiratory rate, moist rales/whistling sounds in the lungs, or tracheal retractions; Radiological evidence (X-ray/CT): signs of pneumonia/bronchitis (e.g., patchy infiltrates, atelectasis). Exclusion criteria: Incomplete clinical data, incomplete pathogen detection results, or duplicate records. Clinical data from 1,431,696 individuals undergoing respiratory pathogen screening were collected in this study. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we excluded entries with incomplete pathogen detection, removed duplicate data from repeated hospitalizations and repeated outpatient visits (1,331,565 cases), as well as duplicate data between outpatient and inpatient records (18,157 cases). Ultimately, a total of 81,974 subjects were included in the statistical analysis (Figure 1).Figure 1Flowchart of the study.Flowchart illustrating a retrospective study design, showing data collection from seven medical institutions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, cohort selection process, analysis dimensions, and six key epidemiological outcomes for respiratory pathogen infections.2.2.Data collectionDemographic and clinical data of enrolled cases were collected through the “Xiaoshan Health Data Platform” platform. The determination of infection status was based on any of the following positive test results: positive serum pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, or positive pathogen antigens or nucleic acids detected in respiratory tract samples. This study encompasses six common respiratory pathogens, including FluA, FluB, RSV, ADV, MP, and CP. For all six pathogens, specimen types included nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swabs, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and blood; detection methods included serological IgM assays, antigen detection, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), with the exception that antigen detection was not included for CP. Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. Only patients with complete test results for all six target pathogens were included in the final analysis.Grouping of study subjects: in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for age-stage division and population age stratification, the study subjects were divided into six age groups: 0– < 3 years (infant and toddler group), 3– < 6 years (preschool group), 6– < 12 years (school-age group), 12– < 18 years (adolescence group), 18– < 60 years (adult group), and ≥60 years (older adult(s) group). According to year span, the subjects were divided into three periods: 2018–2019, 2020–2022, and 2023–2025. Seasonal grouping included spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), and winter (December–February of the following year). The chi-square (χ2) two-sided test was used for intergroup comparisons of qualitative data, and a P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.2.3.Statistical analysisData were exported to Excel, and statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.3.2. Normally distributed continuous data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, while non-normally distributed data are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR). Positivity rates for each study period were calculated as the total number of positive cases divided by the total number of tested cases across all years within that period. Count data are presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups were performed using the chi-square test. All tests were two-sided, and the significance level was set at α = 0.05. Calculation formula: Positive rate (%) = (Number of positive cases detected among the screened population / Total number of screened cases) × 100%. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1907370/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study conducts a multi-center retrospective analysis of a total of 81,974 ARTI cases in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025, describing the temporal variations in the epidemic patterns of six major respiratory pathogens before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Our data confirm the rebound phenomenon of pathogen activity observed globally in the post-COVID-19 pandemic era. However, the recovery patterns varied markedly across pathogens: Flu A and MP rebounded rapidly to pre- COVID-19 pandemic levels, whereas RSV and ADV exhibited delayed or incomplete recovery. These divergent trajectories resulted in a reshaped epidemiological landscape, characterized by altered seasonal peaks and shifts in the age groups predominantly affected. These findings have important implications for understanding the complexity of the “immunity debt” hypothesis, optimizing clinical practice, and reconstructing the local surveillance and early-warning system.Research findings indicate that there are significant differences in the inhibitory effects of NPIs on common respiratory pathogens. The positive rates of Influenza A (FluA), Influenza B (FluB), and MP were significantly suppressed during the period of epidemic prevention and control from 2020 to 2022, and then showed a sharp “revenge rebound” from 2023 to 2025. In particular, the positive rate of FluA in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (19.09%) was more than five times that before the COVID-19 pandemic (3.78%), representing a rebound increase of over 11-fold compared with the COVID-19 pandemic period (1.57%). This phenomenon is consistent with reports from many countries around the world and is widely attributed to the “immunity debt,” that is, NPIs led to a decrease in natural infections among the population and an accumulation of susceptible individuals. Once the interventions were lifted, the pathogens spread rapidly among the population with immunity gaps (7, 10, 11).However, the decline in the positive rates of ADV, CP, and RSV in this study challenges the view that the single “immune debt” hypothesis can universally explain the dynamics of all pathogens, and reveals the “asymmetry” of the impact of NPIs (12). This disparity is the result of the combined effects of pathogen characteristics, population immunodynamics, and persistent changes in behavioral patterns after the pandemic. Taking ADV as an example, it has multiple transmission routes such as droplet, fecal-oral, and contact (13), this niche breadth may have buffered the impact of NPIs, preventing the complete interruption of its transmission during the pandemic and thus avoiding the accumulation of a large susceptible population like that of influenza viruses and MP (14). The latter two are highly dependent on droplet transmission and are strongly suppressed under NPIs, which in turn leads to a “revenge epidemic” after the lifting of the interventions. It is worth noting that the interpretation of the “decline in the positive rate” requires extra caution. Although the positive rates of ADV, CP, and RSV show a persistent state of inhibition, the absolute number of detected cases during the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025) far exceeds the pre-COVID-19 pandemic level (15–17). This strongly suggests that the simple positive rate may underestimate the actual intensity of community transmission and disease burden of this pathogen in the post-COVID-19 pandemic stage. The reasons for this phenomenon may include: the recovery and increase in the overall number of medical consultations after the pandemic, the improvement in the willingness to undergo testing, and the sample dilution effect caused by the co-circulation with other pathogens (such as MP, FluA) (18, 19). Therefore, our data indicate that the evolution of respiratory pathogens in the “post-pandemic era” is not simply a “return to the baseline,” but rather a profound “restructuring of ecological niches.” With their high transmission efficiency, MP and influenza viruses have significantly increased their epidemiological weight in the context of expanded susceptible pools and the restoration of transmission conditions; while other pathogens have their activity levels reshaped either due to their transmission characteristics or because of sustained behavioral suppression (20). This suggests that in the surveillance during the “post-COVID-19 pandemic era,” it is necessary to combine multi-dimensional indicators such as the positive rate and the absolute number of cases, and take into account confounding factors such as changes in medical seeking behavior to more accurately assess the real epidemic situation and disease burden of various pathogens.The stratified outpatient-inpatient comparison further illustrates how healthcare-seeking behavior shapes surveillance data. The universal lower inpatient positivity rate across age groups likely reflects that inpatients include more non-infectious admissions and prior antibiotic use. The widening gap post- COVID-19 pandemic suggests a surge in mild community infections seeking outpatient care. Notably, RSV and ADV were higher in inpatients, consistent with their tendency to cause more severe disease requiring hospitalization (21, 22).This study clearly identifies that MP has become the pathogen with the highest positive rate (19.56%) among ARTI cases in the Hangzhou area, far exceeding that of FluA (16.93%). Age distribution analysis showed that MP infection peaked in children aged 6– < 12 years (38.31%), consistent with recent reports from multiple domestic regions (23, 24). The higher overall positivity of MP compared to RSV in our cohort reflects their distinct age-specific ecological niches rather than diminished clinical relevance of RSV. Age-stratified analysis (Table 4) revealed that MP positivity increased markedly with age, peaking in school-aged children (6– < 12 years: 38.31%), whereas RSV activity was concentrated in infants and toddlers (< 3 years: 5.30%). In older age groups, MP positivity far exceeded RSV (e.g., 6– < 12 years: 38.31% vs. 0.82%), which explains why MP appears more prevalent in the all-ages cohort. RSV remains a critical pathogen causing severe lower respiratory tract infections predominantly in young children, and its importance should not be underestimated despite the lower overall positivity rate in this study. The high susceptibility of 6– < 12 years old can be explained by aspects such as their group living characteristics, immune system development features, and social behavior traits. As semi-enclosed and high-density environments, schools provide ideal conditions for the transmission of MP through droplets. Meanwhile, since children's immune systems are not fully developed and their specific immune memory of MP is relatively limited, these factors collectively make this population the primary victims of MP infection (25).In addition, research has found that the mixed infection pattern (accounting for 17.8% of the total positive cases) provides important clues for understanding the severity of the disease. FluA + MP is the most predominant co-infection combination (accounting for 53.82% of all multiple infections), and this phenomenon deserves high-level attention. Basic research suggests that influenza virus infection can damage respiratory epithelial cells and disrupt the function of the mucosal barrier, thereby creating favorable conditions for the secondary colonization and infection of pathogens such as MP (26). Clinically, co-infection of influenza and mycoplasma may be associated with a longer fever duration, a higher risk of pulmonary imaging progression, and more complex treatment decisions (27). Our data indicate that such co-infections are more prevalent in winter, coinciding with the influenza season. This suggests that during the influenza season, for patients diagnosed with influenza, especially child patients, the possibility of MP co-infection should be vigilant to avoid missed diagnos…
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionAcute Respiratory Tract Infection (ARTI) is a leading cause of outpatient visits and emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and substantial disease burden globally. The pathogen spectrum of ARTI is complex and encompasses viruses, bacteria, and atypical pathogens (1). In China, ARTI is a prevalent infectious disease, which can lead to severe clinical consequences, especially among children, the older adult(s), and individuals with underlying diseases (2). Clarifying the epidemic characteristics of pathogens in specific periods and regions holds crucial scientific value for guiding empirical clinical treatment, implementing precise public health intervention measures (such as vaccination and seasonal prevention), and establishing effective monitoring and early warning systems.In recent years, the epidemic patterns of respiratory pathogens have changed. The global pandemic of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) that began at the end of 2019, along with the widespread implementation of Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) to contain its spread, such as wearing masks, maintaining social distancing, and restricting gatherings and travel, have profoundly altered the ecological and epidemiological characteristics of common respiratory pathogens (3). Multiple studies have confirmed that during the strict implementation of NPIs, the activity levels of many common respiratory viruses, such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), significantly decreased or even disappeared (4, 5). However, since the gradual adjustment and lifting of NPIs at the end of 2022, new trends have emerged in many parts of the world, including the resurgence of common respiratory pathogen activities, shift in epidemic seasons, and co-circulation or alternating prevalence of multiple pathogen (6). For example, post-COVID-19 pandemic surveillance in Guangdong Province revealed that the peak activity of influenza viruses has advanced, the proportion of MP infections has exceeded the pre-COVID-19 pandemic average, and there are significant age-related differences in pathogen distribution (7). These changes indicate that in the “post-COVID-19 pandemic era,” the original pathogen prevalence patterns based on historical data may no longer be applicable, and there is an urgent need for updates and analyses based on the latest monitoring data.As an important central city and transportation hub in eastern China, Hangzhou has a dense population and high population mobility, making it an ideal sentinel site for monitoring the dynamics of respiratory infectious disease. However, there is currently a lack of systematic, long-term longitudinal research covering the complete cycle before the COVID-19 pandemic, during thepandemic, and after the implementation of “Category B Management for Category B Infectious Diseases” on the epidemiological characteristics of multiple pathogens among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, especially studies that simultaneously cover viruses and atypical pathogens.
