full_text: AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. MATERIALS AND METHODSCollection and purification of LCTG-001SIgA was purified and pooled from the breast milk of 120 lactating individuals, as described previously (13). Briefly, frozen human milk was thawed and clarified through centrifugation and dialyzed in PBS. The supernatant was loaded onto a CaptureSelect IgA Affinity Matrix resin, and IgA was isolated as previously described (13). Pooled elution fractions were dialyzed in PBS and filtered. The final concentration was determined using a spectrophotometer.SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresisTwo micrograms of LCTG-001 was mixed with 4× lithium dodecyl sulfate loading dye and β-mercaptoethanol at 95°C for 10 min. Sample was loaded onto a 4 to 12% bis-tris gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and ran at 100 V for 90 min with Bolt Mops SDS running buffer (Invitrogen). The gel was stained with Coomassie blue for 30 min at room temperature and destained using 40% methanol and 10% acetic acid in water.Neutrophil isolationNeutrophils were isolated from peripheral blood of consenting healthy male and female donors as described previously, using density gradient centrifugation (29, 30). Studies were approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board. Briefly, blood was collected into EDTA-coated tubes via venipuncture. Three milliliters of Histopaque 1119 and 3 ml of Histopaque 1077 were layered in a 15-ml Falcon tube, followed by 6 ml of blood. Samples were centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 30 min at room temperature with no deceleration in an Allegra X-12R centrifuge (Beckman Coulter). The neutrophil layer was collected between the Histopaque layers and red blood cells (RBCs). Neutrophils were diluted in 50 ml of cold polymorphonuclear cell (PMN) buffer [0.5% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.3 mM EDTA (Invitrogen) in Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco)]. Diluted cells were centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. The supernatant was discarded, the pellet was resuspended, and RBCs were lysed using ammonium-chloride-potassium (ACK) lysis buffer [NH4Cl (8.3 g/liter), KHCO3 (1 g/liter), and 0.05 mM EDTA, in sterile distilled H2O]. Cells were incubated with ACK lysis buffer for 5 min with agitation every 30 s. Following incubation, cells were diluted in 50 ml of PMN buffer and centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature, followed by an additional wash with PMN buffer. Cells were resuspended in a final volume of 1 ml in PMN buffer.Cells and virusesHuman adenocarcinoma alveolar basal epithelial (A549) cells [American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)] and human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (ATCC) were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells (ATCC) were maintained in Earle’s minimal essential medium (MEM Earles) containing 10% FBS (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, 1% of 1 M sodium pyruvate, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Hep-2 cells (ATCC) were maintained in minimum essential medium (MEM) containing 10% FBS (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Expi293 cells (Gibco) were maintained at 37°C and 8% CO2 with regular agitation (150 rpm) in Expi293 expression medium (Gibco).A/Netherlands/602/2009 H1N1 (NL/09) and X-31 (gifts from P. Palese, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, NY) were propagated in 10-day-old embryonated chicken eggs as per standard protocols (24). X-31 is a reassortant virus with the internal genes of A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1 (PR8) and the HA and NA of A/Hong Kong/1/1968 H3N2 (HK/68). A/California/04/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09) (gift from P. Palese) and A/seal/QC/FAV869-3/2022 H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b) (gift from Y. Berhane, CFIA, MB) were grown in MDCK cells. Cells were infected at 70% viability at a multiplicity of infection of 0.1 and incubated for 1 hour at 37°C. Following incubation, virus was removed and replaced with 1× infection media [1× MEM (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.6% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 1× MEM amino acids (Gibco), 1× MEM vitamin solution (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX (Gibco), 1× penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), 0.6% sodium bicarbonate, 1× Hepes, and tolylsulfonyl phenylalanyl chloromethyl ketone (TPCK)–treated trypsin (1 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich)]. The supernatant was collected 48 hours following infection by centrifugation at 500g for 5 min. RSV A2 expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP; ViraTree) was grown in Hep-2 cells. E1/E3-deleted HuAd serotype 5 expressing GFP was a gift from Z. Xing (McMaster University, ON).H5N1 2.3.4.4b VLP productionPlasmids encoding the HA and NA from A/seal/QC/FAV869-3/2022 H5N1 were a gift from M. Côté (University of Ottawa, ON). HEK 293T cells were seeded in T150 flasks and transfected with HA and NA plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 240 μl of lipofectamine was incubated with 8 ml of Opti-MEM (Gibco) for 7.5 min. During the incubation, 32 μg of each plasmid was diluted with 8 ml of Opti-MEM. Lipofectamine and plasmid mixtures were combined and incubated at room temperature for 25 min. After the incubation, 10 ml of supplemented DMEM (2% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% GlutaMAX, and 1% Hepes) was added to the transfection mixture and incubated on cells overnight at 37°C and 5% CO2. The next day, media was replaced with DMEM containing 0.3% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX. The cell supernatant was collected 4 days posttransfection and centrifuged at 3000g for 2 min. The pellet was removed, and the supernatant was stored at −80°C.Transmission electron microscopyA 3-μl drop of sample was applied to a formvar-coated copper grid stabilized with a 5-nm carbon film and left for 10 min to allow for the VLPs to settle on the grid. Excess sample was blotted off with filter paper. The grids were then briefly rinsed by immersion in deionized water and blotted dry with filter paper. Then, 3 μl of 1% (aq) uranyl acetate was applied to the grid surface and left for 1 min. Excess stain was removed by blotting with filter paper, and the grid was allowed to dry completely. Imaging of the grids was performed using a TALOS L120C transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating at an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. Images were acquired with a 4K CETA complementary metal-oxide semiconductor camera.Influenza A virus purificationClarified supernatants from IAV-infected MDCK cells or allantoic fluid from embryonated chicken eggs were layered on top of 8 ml of 20% sucrose in NTE [0.5 M NaCl, 10 mM tris HCl, and 1 mM EDTA (pH 7.5)] buffer in Ultra-Clear Ultracentrifuge tubes (Beckman Coulter). Samples were spun for 2 hours at 4°C at 76650g inside a SW 32i rotor using an Optima L-90K Ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). Clarified supernatants from VLP-transfected 293T cells were layered on top of 3 ml of 20% glycerol in PBS in Ultra-Clear Ultracentrifuge tubes (Beckman Coulter). Samples were spun for 4 hours at 4°C at 135,000g inside a SW 32i rotor using an Optima L-90K Ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). Purified viruses and VLPs were quantified using a bicinchoninic acid assay Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.Recombinant antigenscH6/1 HA was a gift from P. Palese (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, NY). cH6/1 is composed of the H6 HA head domain from A/mallard/Sweden/81/02 H6N1 and H1 HA stalk domain from PR8. HK/68 HA was made using the Expi293 expression system. Expi293 cells (Gibco) were transfected with plasmid encoding HK/68 HA (gift from A. McDermott, NIAID, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Proteins were purified by Ni resin affinity chromatography. RSV A2 fusion protein (RSV-F), Cal/09 HA, A/American wigeon/South Carolina/AH0195145/2021 (H5N1) HA, and A/Texas/37/2024 (H5N1) NA were purchased from SinoBiological. Lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells was a gift from Z. Xing (McMaster University, ON).Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assaysThe 96-well NUNC-MaxiSorp plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated overnight at 4°C with purified soluble Cal/09 HA, HK/68 HA, cH6/1 HA, H5 HA, N1 NA, RSV-F recombinant protein, or purified 2.3.4.4b H5N1 VLPs, diluted to 2 μg/ml in bicarbonate-carbonate coating buffer (pH 9.4). For HuAd5 ELISAs, plates were coated with 50 μl of Ad-5–infected HeLa cell lysate (100 μg/ml) in PBS. Plates were blocked for 1 hour at 37°C with reagent diluent [0.5% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.02% sodium azide, in 1× tris-Tween buffer]. LCTG-001 was serially diluted 1:2 across each row. For in vivo biodistribution studies, homogenized lung tissue or BAL fluid was serially diluted 1:2 across each row. Following a 1-hour incubation at 37°C, plates were washed three times with 1× tris-Tween wash buffer. After washing, goat anti-human-biotin IgA (Southern Biotech) was diluted 1:2000 in reagent diluent and added to all wells. Plates were again incubated for 1 hour at 37°C, followed by three washes with 1× tris-Tween buffer. A streptavidin-alkaline phosphatase secondary antibody (1:2000, Southern Biotech) was added to all wells for 1 hour at 37°C. Plates were subsequently washed three times before addition of pNPP one component microwell substrate solution (Southern Biotech) to each well. Plates were developed for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with an equal volume 3 N sodium hydroxide. The optical density (OD) at 405 nm was read on a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent). OD values were normalized on the basis of control wells with no sample.MNT assays Human adenovirus MNT The day before infection, 96-well plates of A549 cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 105 cells per well in clear flat-bottom TC-treated 96-well plates (Corning). Cells were subsequently incubated with serial dilutions of LCTG-001 and an E1/E3-deleted HuAd serotype 5 expressing GFP (gift from Z. Xing, McMaster University, Hamilton, ON, Canada) (1.6 × 106 PFU per well) for 24 hours at 37°C and 5% CO2 in α-MEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX (Gibco). Postincubation, fluorescence (GFP) was read using Cytation 5 (Agilent, Biotek). Neutralization titer was determined as the highest antibody dilution that achieved a 50% reduction in fluorescence compared to the virus control wells. Respiratory syncytial virus MNT The day before infection, Hep-2 cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 104 cells per well in clear flat-bottom TC-treated 96-well plates (Corning). Cells were subsequently incubated with serial dilutions of LCTG-001 and RSV GFP (ViraTree) (4 × 103 PFU per well) for 1 hour at 37°C, 5% CO2. The antibody/virus mixture was removed and replenished with fresh DMEM supplemented with 2% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% Hepes (pH 7.3), and 1% GlutaMAX for 24 hours at 37°C, 5% CO2. Postincubation, fluorescence (GFP) was read using Cytation 5 (Agilent, Biotek). Neutralization titer was determined as the highest antibody dilution that achieved a 50% reduction in fluorescence compared to the virus control wells. Influenza A virus MNT The day before infection, 96-well plates of MDCK cells were seeded at a density of 5 × 104 cells per well in clear flat-bottom TC-treated 96-well plates (Corning). Serial dilution of LCTG-001 and viruses (3600 PFU Cal/09 or 24500 PFU X-31) were preincubated for 30 min at 37°C and 5% CO2 in DMEM supplemented with 0.3% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), and TPCK (1 μg/ml)–treated trypsin (Sigma-Aldrich). Following incubation, MDCK cells were infected with the LCTG-001–virus mixture for 1 hour at 37°C and 5% CO2. After the 1-hour infection, the infectious media was replaced with fresh supplemented DMEM. Plates were incubated for 18 hours and then fixed with 80% acetone for 20 min at −20°C before blocking with 5% nonfat milk in PBS for 30 min at room temperature, followed by an incubation in 3% hydrogen peroxide for 20 min at room temperature. Plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer before a 1-hour incubation at room temperature with a 1:2000 dilution of biotin-conjugated mouse anti-NP (Millipore) in 5% nonfat milk. Following incubation, plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer and incubated for 1 hour at room temperature with a secondary horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–conjugated streptavidin (1:5000, Millipore). Plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer before the addition of SigmaFast OPD (Sigma-Aldrich) to each well. Plates were developed for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with an equal volume of 3 M hydrochloric acid. The OD at 490 nm was read on a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent). OD values were normalized on the basis of uninfected control wells, and percent neutralization was calculated on the basis of the ratio between the sample OD value to infected control values.Enzyme-linked lectin assaysThe 96-well NUNC-MaxiSorp plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated overnight at 4°C with fetuin (25 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich) diluted in 1× KPL coating buffer (SeraCare). In a separate plate, LCTG-001 was serially diluted in sample diluent [MES (Life Technologies) (pH 6.5), 20 mM CaCl2, 1% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5% Tween 20]. Virus (Cal/09, X-31, or H5N1 VLPs) was diluted to 90% of the max OD (predetermined) in sample diluent. Fetuin-coated plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer, and LCTG-001 dilutions and virus were transferred to the fetuin-coated plate. Plates were incubated overnight at 37°C. Following incubation, plates were washed six times with PBS-Tween wash buffer. Peanut agglutinin (PNA)–HRP (1 mg/ml) was diluted 1:500 in PNA-HRP diluent [MES (pH 6.5), 20 mM CaCl2, and 1% BSA] and added to all wells for 2 hours at room temperature. Plates were then washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer before the addition of SigmaFast OPD (Sigma-Aldrich) to each well. Plates were developed for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with an equal volume of 3 M hydrochloric acid. The OD at 490 nm was read on a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent). OD values were normalized on the basis of control wells without virus, and percent inhibition was calculated on the basis of the ratio between the sample OD value to control values with virus only.Luminol assaysLuminol assays were performed as previously described (30). Briefly, immune complexes were formed by incubating 2.5 μg of virus with 5 μg of LCTG-001 in 50 μl for 30 min at room temperature. Luminol (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to all wells. Following isolation, 5 × 105 cells of human neutrophils were added to each well. Kinetic measurements of luminescence [in relative light units (RLU)] were taken at 1-min intervals for 1 hour using a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent).MiceEight- to 12-week-old female BALB/c mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratories (Saint Constant, QC, Canada). B cell–deficient mice C.Cg-Igh-Jtm1Dhu of BALB/c background were purchased from Taconic Biosciences (Germantown, NY, USA). Animals were housed under specific pathogen–free conditions at McMaster University, Hamilton, ON. All animal protocols were reviewed and approved by the institutional Animal Research and Ethics Board (Animal Utilization Protocol 23-62).Antibody administration and IAV infectionAnimals received LCTG-001, PBS, and NL/09 intranasally as previously described (70). For antibody administration, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane and received a single bolus of 40 μl containing either 1 mg of LCTG-001 diluted in PBS or PBS as a negative control. Mice were infected with 450 PFU of NL/09, administered intranasally in a final volume of 40 μl diluted in PBS. Mice were monitored for weight loss and clinical signs daily, including huddling, lack of grooming, and lethargy. A reduction to 80% of initial weight was considered humane endpoint in accordance with institutional guidelines.Lung isolation and preparation for histologyMice were euthanized by exsanguination. Whole lungs were isolated as previously described (70), with some modifications. Briefly, lungs were removed from the mice and cannulated. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSAssessment of broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogensUnlike IgG in conventional IVIG or convalescent plasma, which is peripherally sourced from the circulation, SIgA is exclusively found at mucosal sites. Sourcing from the respiratory mucosa is not feasible due to procedural complexities and limited antibody yield. To circumvent these limitations, we explored breast milk as an alternative source of mucosal SIgA. Breast milk is a scalable and sustainable source of mucosal SIgA, and donations of extra breast milk are already collected by over 700 human milk banks worldwide. To produce purified SIgA, breast milk samples were collected from 120 lactating donors through collaborations with milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Initial sample shipments included 85 donor contributions received on 11 October 2022, followed by an additional 35 samples on 29 November 2022. The samples, collected throughout 2022, were pooled to yield a total volume of 15,585 ml. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. The purity of LCTG-001 was confirmed by Coomassie staining (fig. S1) and was consistent with previous reports (13). The donor cohort was not screened for recent infection or vaccination status, thereby aligning with conventional IVIG collection practices in which donors are not selected on the basis of prior antigenic exposures (3, 14).We next evaluated whether the polyclonal SIgA pool, LCTG-001, could recognize and neutralize a panel of respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human adenovirus (HuAd), and IAV. Representative strains and serotypes were selected for each virus to assess LCTG-001’s binding and neutralizing potency. To assess LCTG-001’s antiviral activity, we performed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to evaluate antibody binding, alongside microneutralization (MNT) assays to measure functional neutralization.We first assessed binding of LCTG-001 to RSV fusion protein (RSV-F), the antigen used in licensed RSV vaccines (15). LCTG-001 demonstrated robust binding to RSV-F (AUC = 62.02 ± 1.273; Fig. 1A), and these antibodies were able to neutralize RSV at physiologically relevant concentrations [median inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 320 μg/ml; Fig. 1B].Fig. 1.LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogens.(A, C, and E) LCTG-001 binding responses to RSV-F (A), HuAd5 lysate (C), and Cal/09 HA (E). (B, D, and F) LCTG-001 neutralizing antibody responses to RSV (B), HuAd5 (D), and Cal/09 (F), measured by percent (%) neutralization using MNT assays. Data presented in (A) to (F) represent mean ± SEM. Data presented in (A), (C), and (E) represent three technical replicates. Data presented in (B), (D), and (F) are from three independent experiments.We next assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against adenovirus, focusing on HuAd type 5 (HuAd5), one of the most prevalent HuAd serotypes (16, 17). ELISAs were performed using the lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells as a source of antigen (18). Again, LCTG-001 demonstrated specific binding to the lysate of infected cells (AUC = 62.28 ± 2.309; Fig. 1C) and neutralized HuAd5 with considerable potency (IC50 = 180 μg/ml; Fig. 1D).Last, we assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against IAV. IAV is a respiratory virus responsible for both seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics, with five pandemics in the last century (19). We first investigated the ability of LCTG-001 to recognize and neutralize A/California/07/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09). Cal/09 (H1N1) is an isolate from the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which then circulated seasonally and was a recommended seasonal influenza vaccine strain for more than 5 years in North America. Hence, most of the population has been exposed through infection and/or vaccination. Similar to RSV and HuAd5, LCTG-001 showed specific binding to Cal/09 (H1N1) hemagglutinin (HA) (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E) and neutralization activity (IC50 = 670 μg/ml; Fig. 1F). Antibody responses generated by infection or vaccination primarily target the immunodominant HA head, which can significantly vary between strains. Unlike the variable HA head, the stalk domain is relatively conserved, with stalk-specific antibodies capable of providing protection against diverse IAV strains (20). However, stalk-specific antibody responses are typically low in magnitude but tend to increase with age and influenza virus exposures (21, 22). Despite this, these antibodies can provide broad protection by targeting conserved stalk epitopes, particularly in the context of vaccine mismatch or exposure to novel pandemic strains where HA head-specific immunity is lacking. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONIn this study, we evaluated the antiviral activity and protective efficacy of LCTG-001, a polyclonal SIgA product derived from pooled human breast milk, as a novel mucosal passive immunization strategy that can address the inherent limitations associated with conventional intravenous, IgG-based treatments. IVIG and monoclonal antibody passive immunization strategies, while standard of care in the field for conferring prophylactic and/or therapeutic protection against respiratory pathogens, often have limited transudation to the respiratory mucosa (36–39). These therapies are also logistically burdensome due to the need for parenteral administration in health care settings and are associated with a variety of side effects, including infusion-related reactions (40).In contrast to the periphery, the predominant antibody isotype found in the respiratory mucosa is SIgA. SIgA is actively transported across epithelial barriers and is highly resistant to proteolytic degradation, making it well suited for conferring protection within the respiratory mucosa (41). Moreover, SIgA is naturally localized to mucosa through polymeric immunoglobulin receptor–mediated epithelial transport, depositing IgA into the lumen where respiratory viruses establish infection, a targeted delivery that serum-derived IgG achieves only sparingly (11, 39, 41, 42).Our results demonstrate that LCTG-001 has broad-spectrum antiviral activity mediated by multiple mechanisms. This polyclonal SIgA neutralized diverse respiratory viruses, including RSV, adenovirus, and representatives of both circulating human group 1 and group 2 IAV subtypes, including those with pandemic potential, thereby highlighting its exceptionally broad reactivity. Similarly, polyclonal SIgA compositions administered via the intranasal and intratracheal route were able to neutralize SARS-CoV-2 in K18+ hACE2 transgenic mice (13). This breadth of activity likely arises from the rich and diverse pool of SIgA isolated from pooled breast milk, capturing a wide array of antibodies with varying specificities within a single product.Notably, LCTG-001 not only inhibited IAV viral entry in vitro but also exhibited robust NA inhibition. While NA antibodies may not be potently neutralizing, they can limit viral spread and have been shown to correlate with protection in influenza infection (43–45). Both HA stalk binding and NA-specific antibodies can contribute to NAI activity, the former through steric hindrance of the NA binding site and the latter by directly binding near the enzymatic site of the protein (26, 27). The presence of NAI activity suggests that LCTG-001 can impair virion release, even in the context of strains for which conventional neutralizing antibodies are absent. Furthermore, LCTG-001 induced Fc-dependent activation of neutrophils, as evidenced by a luminol-based assay. In humans, IgA is known to engage FcαRI (CD89) on myeloid cells, triggering processes like phagocytosis, respiratory burst, and NETosis (29, 30). Our data confirm that a complex SIgA pool from breast milk can harness this pathway. Thus, beyond classical neutralization, LCTG-001 is capable of activating innate immune cells to facilitate pathogen clearance. The ability of SIgA to activate neutrophils has important implications for mucosal defense. IgA is often viewed as a non-inflammatory “shield” that blocks pathogen entry. Here, we show that SIgA can also engage innate immunity, further facilitating pathogen clearance. This FcαRI-dependent mechanism adds a crucial layer of protection at mucosal surfaces.Our use of a polyclonal human SIgA pool from breast milk reveals the breadth of Fc-mediated activity of LCTG-001 in the context of IAV. Prior studies have mostly examined serum-derived or engineered monomeric IgA (29, 30, 46). SIgA can engage the FcαR on cells; however, this interaction requires accessory molecules such as MAC-1 and results in a lower affinity compared to cross-linked monomeric IgA (47–49). Hence, the ability of SIgA to engage Fc-mediated neutrophil effector functions in an IAV antigen–specific context has not been fully examined. We demonstrated that the polyclonal SIgA which comprises LCTG-001 retains the ability to engage Fc effector functions on neutrophils, triggering a potent effector response against three different strains of IAV. This novel finding further broadens the paradigm of how SIgA contributes to antiviral immunity, indicating that SIgA-based interventions could actively modulate the innate immune milieu in the airways during respiratory viral infection.Another notable aspect of LCTG-001’s efficacy is its breadth of antiviral activities against IAVs. Our data suggest that this polyclonal mixture appears to target multiple viral proteins and life cycle steps: We detected antibodies likely directed against the conserved HA stalk, those capable of inhibiting NA (mediating NAI), and antibodies capable of stimulating Fc-dependent effector functions. These modes of action are complementary, and the interplay between Fab-mediated and Fc-mediated functions is evident in our data. In essence, LCTG-001 may not rely on a single mechanism of action but rather uses a variety of effector functions to mediate protection against viral pathogens. This was evident after H1N1 challenge, where there was incomplete neutralization at the highest concentration of antibody tested. Despite this, we observed high binding activity to Cal/09 (H1N1) HA. The robust protection may be partially explained by the high level of NA inhibition and Fc-mediated neutrophil activity against Cal/09 (H1N1), which suggests the presence of antibodies with potent anti-IAV activity that may not demonstrate traditional neutralization in vitro. These diverse activities may be especially valuable for highly mutable viruses like IAV, where complete protection often requires neutralizing the virus as well as containing infection through immune effector mechanisms (3, 50–52).The cross-reactivity of LCTG-001 against an H5N1 avian influenza strain (clade 2.3.4.4b), despite no known exposure of donors to this strain, was particularly encouraging. These antibodies appear to be directed against the conserved group 1 HA stalk of H5 and to the N1 protein. This result suggests that the pool of human donor SIgA contains antibodies recognizing conserved epitopes shared with emerging avian viruses. VLPs were used to allow for work to be completed under standard biosafety level 2 conditions. Although VLPs generally preserve many of the structural and antigenic features of the wild-type virus, differences in particle assembly, glycosylation patterns, protein stoichiometry, and membrane composition can alter the presentation and accessibility of antigenic epitopes (53). Still, likely candidates for such cross-reactive targets are the HA stalk and NA (54, 55), as was confirmed by the observed binding activity of LCTG-001 to both recombinant HA and NA from 2.3.4.4b (H5N1). Through repeated infections or vaccinations with common IAV strains, antibodies likely accumulate in the breast milk that recognize conserved elements of potential pandemic viruses, in agreement with studies reporting cross-reactive serum IgG in humans (54, 56, 57). While these cross-reactive antibodies may not potently neutralize a novel strain, they can contribute to protection via secondary mechanisms such as by inhibiting the NA activity of the virus or by engaging Fc receptors for virus clearance. LCTG-001 could serve as a readily deployable passive immunization strategy in the face of an emerging influenza pandemic by providing immediate partial immunity while strain-specific vaccines or monoclonals are being developed. Even partial protection, by constricting viral replication or dampening undesired inflammation, could be life-saving during an outbreak of a novel virus, especially for immunocompromised individuals. full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONImmunoglobulin replacement therapy, which can take the form of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or subcutaneous immunoglobulin, is essential for mitigating infectious diseases and is especially critical in treating primary immunodeficiencies such as common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID is characterized by impaired antibody production, manifesting as reduced levels of immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgA, and/or IgM (1, 2). Regular IVIG infusions are administered to patients with CVID to replenish immunoglobulin levels, thereby reducing infection frequency and severity (3). Despite its effectiveness, IVIG therapy is costly, invasive, and requires frequent medically assisted administration (1, 4).Beyond management of immunoglobulin immunodeficiencies, IVIG and convalescent plasma have also been used as passive immunization strategies to protect populations against viral infections, including in pandemic settings where vaccines are either unavailable or in limited supply. This was exemplified during the 1918 and 2009 influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics, as well as during the initial stages of COVID-19 (5–8). However, these strategies require intravenous administration of antibodies derived from the circulation, which are rich in IgG and monomeric IgA but differ markedly from the predominantly dimeric and secretory IgA (SIgA) present at mucosal surfaces (9). Thus, these approaches do not fully recapitulate the protective immune landscape of the respiratory mucosa found in healthy individuals (4, 10). In addition, antibodies administered intravenously must transudate from the circulation to the mucosal surfaces to exert their protective effects, which limits availability at respiratory surfaces (11). This limitation highlights the need for mucosally delivered passive immunization strategies which can deliver antibodies directly to the site of pathogen entry.Sourcing SIgA from human biospecimens, such as those found in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluids, is not practical due to the invasiveness of the procedures and the limited yield of antibodies. In contrast, breast milk is a more attractive source that is more plentiful, accessible, and rich in mucosal SIgA (12). Previous work has demonstrated that breast milk–derived SIgA has antiviral activity against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and is a viable prophylactic strategy in preclinical models (13). This study used breast milk from human milk donors post–SARS-CoV-2 infection, thereby enriching the antibody pool for anti–SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. Building on these observations, we hypothesized that purifying IgA from a large sample of donors without screening milk samples for neutralizing antibodies against any particular pathogen would yield a polyclonal SIgA product with broad antiviral activity against a diverse array of respiratory pathogens due to varied donor exposures to infections and/or vaccinations, akin to IVIG.Here, we investigate a polyclonal, breast milk–derived SIgA product, LCTG-001. Our findings demonstrate that LCTG-001 exhibits broad antiviral activity in vitro against a panel of respiratory pathogens. We further demonstrate that LCTG-001 has neutralizing and nonneutralizing activity against both group 1 and group 2 IAVs, in addition to activity against emerging zoonotic strains. Last, we demonstrate that when delivered directly to the respiratory mucosa, LCTG-001 was protective in vivo against IAV challenge in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. Collectively, these results highlight mucosal delivery of breast milk–derived IgA as a passive immunization strategy capable of addressing limitations inherent in traditional intravenous antibody therapies, offering potential protection against both endemic and pandemic respiratory infections. full_text_excerpt: These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. full_text: AbstractObjectiveThe aim of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics of severe viral encephalitis (SVE) in children and to identify exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality, thereby providing preliminary evidence to facilitate early risk stratification and reduce SVE-related disability and mortality.MethodsA retrospective study was conducted in 75 children diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, including 50 mild cases and 25 SVE cases. Demographic data, clinical manifestations, and laboratory parameters (peripheral white blood cell count (WBC), serum sodium, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leukocyte and protein levels, serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE), electroencephalography (EEG), neuroimaging findings, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores) were collected and compared between groups. Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses, with enteroviruses (EVs) being the predominant type, accounting for 7 cases, followed by herpes zoster virus (VZV) and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases. In the SVE group, 9 out of 25 cases (36%) were found to have pathogens, with influenza A virus (4 cases) and herpes simplex virus (2 cases) being the main ones. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality (primary outcome) within the SVE subgroup.ResultsAmong the 25 children with SVE (15 males, mean age 7.74 ± 2.2 years), fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common; four patients died (16%). Compared with children with mild encephalitis, the SVE group exhibited significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05). However, there were no significant differences in CSF leukocytes, CSF protein, blood leukocytes, or serum sodium. In univariate Firth-corrected logistic regression, neuroimaging abnormalities (P = 0.007), seizures (P = 0.011), EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018), lower GCS score (per 1-point decrease, P < 0.001), and higher serum NSE (per 10 ng/mL increment, P = 0.018) were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality.ConclusionPediatric SVE presents with nonspecific early symptoms and substantial mortality. Seizures, EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality. However, given the small sample size and single-center design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multi-center prospective cohorts. Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment.Keywords: children, clinical characteristics, exploratory factors, in-hospital mortality, severe viral encephalitis 2.Subjects and methods2.1.Study subjectsAll cases were derived from pediatric inpatients diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital from January 2023 to December 2025. All enrolled children fulfilled comprehensive diagnostic criteria for viral encephalitis as follows: (1) Acute onset of neurological symptoms and signs; (2) CSF examination showing an elevated WBC count (> 10 × 106/L) with a predominance of lymphocytes, and/or a mild increase in protein; (3) Electroencephalogram and/or cranial imaging showing changes consistent with viral encephalitis; (4) Other central nervous system diseases such as purulent meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and autoimmune encephalitis were excluded. Pediatric GCS scores were independently assigned and cross-validated by two assessors (physicians and nurses). All assessors had passed the standardized training and assessment within the department. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveThe aim of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics of severe viral encephalitis (SVE) in children and to identify exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality, thereby providing preliminary evidence to facilitate early risk stratification and reduce SVE-related disability and mortality.MethodsA retrospective study was conducted in 75 children diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, including 50 mild cases and 25 SVE cases. Demographic data, clinical manifestations, and laboratory parameters (peripheral white blood cell count (WBC), serum sodium, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leukocyte and protein levels, serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE), electroencephalography (EEG), neuroimaging findings, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores) were collected and compared between groups. Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses, with enteroviruses (EVs) being the predominant type, accounting for 7 cases, followed by herpes zoster virus (VZV) and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases. In the SVE group, 9 out of 25 cases (36%) were found to have pathogens, with influenza A virus (4 cases) and herpes simplex virus (2 cases) being the main ones. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality (primary outcome) within the SVE subgroup.ResultsAmong the 25 children with SVE (15 males, mean age 7.74 ± 2.2 years), fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common; four patients died (16%). Compared with children with mild encephalitis, the SVE group exhibited significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05). However, there were no significant differences in CSF leukocytes, CSF protein, blood leukocytes, or serum sodium. In univariate Firth-corrected logistic regression, neuroimaging abnormalities (P = 0.007), seizures (P = 0.011), EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018), lower GCS score (per 1-point decrease, P < 0.001), and higher serum NSE (per 10 ng/mL increment, P = 0.018) were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality.ConclusionPediatric SVE presents with nonspecific early symptoms and substantial mortality. Seizures, EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality. However, given the small sample size and single-center design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multi-center prospective cohorts. Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment.Keywords: children, clinical characteristics, exploratory factors, in-hospital mortality, severe viral encephalitis

full_text_sections.results: 2.2.2.Routine laboratory indicators (initial test results)1) Peripheral blood test: White blood cell (WBC) count—a significantly elevated or decreased count may indicate severe disease. 2) Serum sodium: hyponatremia, especially < 130 mmol/L, strongly suggests possible syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which is a marker of increased intracranial pressure and disease worsening. 3) Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: WBC count—a high count does not necessarily indicate more severe disease; Protein content—a significant elevation (> 1 g/L) indicates severe disruption of the blood-brain barrier. 3.Results3.1.General characteristicsAmong the 50 children with mild viral encephalitis, there were 27 males and 23 females, with a mean age of 5.8 ± 2.2 years. Mild cases occurred year-round; 21 (42%) presented in winter-spring (December-May) and 29 (58%) in summer-autumn (June-November). Among the 25 SVE patients, there were 15 males and 10 females, with a mean age of 7.74 ± 2.2 years. SVE also occurred throughout the year, with 17 cases (68%) in winter-spring and 8 cases (32%) in summer-autumn. Acute onset (≤ 7 days) was observed in 23 cases (92%), and subacute onset (> 7 days) in 2 cases (8%). Compared with the mild viral encephalitis group, the SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates and lower GCS scores (all P < 0.05), while the incidence of fever was not significantly different between the two groups (P > 0.05). See Table 1.All 75 children (50 mild, 25 SVE) underwent blood and CSF sampling for pathogen detection using multiplex PCR and/or serum virus IgM antibody tests. Additionally, throat swabs for respiratory virus PCR were collected for all patients. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses. Among them, 7 cases were infected with enteroviruses (EVs), followed by VZV and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases; 1 case of influenza A virus; 1 case of parainfluenza virus; and 1 case of EBV. Among the 25 SVE patients, 4 were infected with influenza A, 2 with HSV, 1 with SARS-CoV-2, 1 with human parainfluenza, 1 with adenovirus, and the remaining cases had no specific virus identified (clinical diagnosis was accepted as per the criteria described in Methods).3.2.Clinical symptoms and signs (SVE)Fever was the most frequent clinical symptom, observed in 19 out of 25 patients (76%), followed by signs of elevated intracranial pressure (e.g., headache and vomiting) in 17 patients (68%). Neurological dysfunction, including limb shaking, unsteady gait, hemiplegia, or slurred speech, was the initial manifestation in 8 patients (32%). Respiratory symptoms occurred during the disease course in 15 patients (60%). Psychobehavioral abnormalities, mainly excitatory symptoms such as irritability and delirium, were present in 6 patients (24%). Altered consciousness was observed in 11 patients (44%), and cognitive impairment was noted in a small proportion of cases (8%). Seizures occurred in 14 patients, predominantly as generalized seizures.3.3.Comparison of laboratory indicators between pediatric SVE and mild viral encephalitisCompared with the mild viral encephalitis group, the SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher rates of seizures, and lower GCS scores (all P < 0.05). Regarding laboratory indicators, the SVE group showed significantly higher rates of EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, and serum NSE levels than the mild encephalitis group (all P < 0.05). Among the 25 patients with SVE, 22 underwent cranial MRI and 3 underwent cranial CT because of their clinical condition. Eleven patients (44%) had abnormal neuroimaging findings: 10 on MRI and 1 on CT. MRI abnormalities presented as single or multiple patchy or band-like long T1 and long T2 signals, and some were accompanied by inflammatory demyelination. The MRI lesions involved the unilateral insular lobe in 4 cases, the brainstem in 2, the cerebellum in 1, the bilateral frontal lobes in 4, and extensive brain parenchyma in 2. EEG was abnormal in 21 cases: 11 showed paroxysmal diffuse high-amplitude slow waves, and 10 had focal epileptic discharges. However, no significant differences were observed in CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, blood leukocyte count, or serum sodium (all P > 0.05). See Table 2.3.4.Univariate comparisons and firth-penalized logistic regression for factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVEThe primary outcome for this analysis was in-hospital mortality (death versus survival during hospitalization). Among continuous variables, the death group had significantly lower GCS scores (P = 0.001) and significantly higher serum NSE levels (P = 0.007) compared with the survival group. No significant differences were observed in length of fever, CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, peripheral blood WBC, or serum sodium between the two groups (all P > 0.05).Among the examined variables, neuroimaging abnormalities showed the strongest association with mortality (P = 0.007), followed by seizures (P = 0.011) and EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018). Similarly, each 10 ng/mL increment in serum NSE was associated with an increased in-hospital mortality risk (P = 0.018). The odds ratio for GCS is interpreted per 1-point decrease in the score (lower GCS → higher mortality risk). The odds ratio for NSE is interpreted per 10 ng/mL increment. No significant associations were found for length of fever, CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, peripheral blood WBC count, or serum sodium (all P > 0.10). These differences reflect clinical judgment and severity at presentation rather than a randomized treatment effect. There were 2 cases of epilepsy and 1 case of decreased lower limb muscle strength among survivors; there were 4 deaths. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionViral encephalitis arises from viral invasion of the intracranial compartment, triggering diffuse parenchymal brain inflammation. Early clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and may be limited to non-specific symptoms including fever, headache, fatigue, and myalgia (12). The incidence of viral encephalitis shows a seasonal pattern, with peaks from June to July and from December to January (13), which is similar to the pattern observed in this study. The winter-spring predominance in our cohort may reflect the circulation pattern of respiratory viruses such as influenza and adenovirus, which constituted the majority of identified pathogens in this study. Unlike the classic predominance of enteroviruses reported in other pediatric encephalitis cohorts (14), our findings suggest that respiratory viruses may play a more prominent role in severe encephalitis cases during the winter-spring season in our region. Furthermore, we found that the age of children with severe encephalitis in Anqing was slightly older than that of those with mild conditions. In the present cohort, the pathogen detection rate among patients with SVE reached 36% (9/25). Influenza-A virus was the most frequently identified pathogen (4/25, 16%), followed by herpes simplex virus (2/25, 8%). This distribution was different from the classic pattern reported in the literature. It is possible that during this period, the enterovirus may not be the predominant circulating strain in this region. The sensitivity of viral nucleic acid testing is influenced by various factors such as sampling time, primer design, and viral load, approximately 40% to 60% of clinical cases of viral encephalitis have no identifiable pathogen, as documented in the literature (14).In recent years, the onset of viral encephalitis has shown a trend toward younger age groups, with increased incidence in neonates and infants (15). If not diagnosed and treated promptly, children may develop severe neurological complications (16); therefore, early and accurate diagnosis is crucial for improving prognosis. In most cases, mild viral encephalitis has a good prognosis after active treatment, whereas severe viral encephalitis progresses rapidly, is more likely to cause other CNS symptoms, leads to sequelae, and can even result in death (7). Clinically, brain failure is common in severe viral encephalitis and is an important cause of death in pediatric intensive care units. In the acute phase of pediatric SVE, various symptoms may occur, including agitation, drowsiness, coma, neurological dysfunction, convulsions, and psychobehavioral abnormalities. The most common clinical symptoms of SVE are headache, decreased consciousness, and convulsions, and in most cases the viral etiology remains unknown (3, 12), which is consistent with the clinical presentation of SVE patients in this study. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a rapid indicator of the severity of brain injury and plays an important role in determining patient prognosis. In the present study, univariate analyses demonstrated that children with SVE who died exhibited significantly lower GCS scores and higher serum NSE concentrations compared with survivors. Neuroimaging abnormalities were also markedly more prevalent among non-survivors. These observations align with prior reports demonstrating that the magnitude of brain injury reflected by GCS, NSE, and neuroimaging is tightly associated with prognosis in viral encephalitis (7, 17). Pratamastuti D et al. found that the median serum NSE level in the acute encephalitis syndrome was significantly higher than that of the non-acute encephalitis syndrome group, these results indicate that serum NSE was a good indicator of neuronal brain injury (18). Similarly, in our study, serum NSE levels were higher in children with SVE than in those with mild viral encephalitis, and elevated serum NSE was identified as an exploratory factor associated with in-hospital mortality. Abnormal EEG and neuroimaging findings, as well as high NSE levels, reflect the extent of brain tissue injury and help assess patient prognosis.In the present study, most children with SVE received combined corticosteroid and immunoglobulin therapy, and the overall recovery rate was relatively high. In this cohort, immunomodulatory therapy was more frequently used in patients with more severe clinical presentations. The observational nature precludes causal inference, but our data provide a real-world snapshot of current management practices for pediatric SVE. In recent years, researchers have increasingly focused on exploring prognosis-associated factors in patients with established SVE, attempting to construct prediction models using clinical symptoms, laboratory indicators, and other parameters (16, 19). Gao et al. found that convulsive status epilepticus, stress-induced hyperglycemia, and miR-125b are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE (20). Song et al. reported that levels of soluble interleukin-2 receptor (SIL-2R), endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), and CD93 in CSF and serum are significantly elevated in children with viral encephalitis and are closely associated with disease progression and prognosis, suggesting their potential value as early warning biomarkers (21). However, current research in this field is still in a preliminary stage, and a unified early warning indicator system with standardized cutoff values has not yet been established, limiting its clinical application and generalization. The key challenge in the clinical management of SVE is the mismatch between the therapeutic time window and the assessment of disease severity. This study demonstrated that seizures, EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE level were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE. However, due to the small sample size (particularly the small number of deaths, n = 4), we were unable to perform multivariable adjustment for potential confounders. Therefore, these associations should be regarded as exploratory and preliminary rather than confirmatory. The extremely wide confidence intervals for categorical variables further reflect the statistical instability inherent in small-sample analyses. Larger multicenter studies with sufficient sample sizes are urgently needed to establish independent exploratory factors and to develop reliable risk stratification tools for pediatric SVE.Treatment modalities for SVE include antiviral drugs, osmotic agents to reduce intracranial pressure, corticosteroid and immunoglobulins, antiepileptic drugs, brain protection, and brain metabolism-enhancing agents. Studies have reported that early use of hemoperfusion combined with continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration may improve the prognosis of pediatric SVE more than hemoperfusion alone (22). The timing of therapy initiation was within 24–48 h of diagnosis, and the indications were based on clinical judgment (rapid neurological deterioration, brain edema on imaging, or refractory seizures). In this cohort, the majority of SVE patients received corticosteroids and/or IVIG, and 84% survived to discharge. However, the observational nature of this study precludes causal inference regarding treatment efficacy. Treatment allocation was based on clinical judgment and disease severity, and differences in treatment between survivors and non-survivors likely reflect confounding by indication. Therefore, the observed association between immunotherapy and survival should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment benefit. Prospective randomized studies are needed to evaluate the efficacy of immunomodulatory therapies in pediatric SVE. The role of immunotherapy in pediatric SVE remains an area of ongoing investigation (23).Several limitations of this study must be acknowledged. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionThe burden of pediatric SVE remains substantial. Early clinical symptoms are non-specific; specific clinical markers and sensitive early-warning tools are lacking, and clinical prognosis is often unfavorable. Convulsive seizures, abnormal EEG findings, neuroimaging abnormalities, elevated serum NSE concentrations, and low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores represent potential factors associated with in-hospital mortality and merit further validation for mortality-risk stratification among children with SVE. Based on the above background, this study describes the clinical characteristics (including demographics, symptoms, signs, laboratory findings, EEG and neuroimaging features) of children with SVE in Anqing City of China, and compares the clinical and laboratory profiles between SVE and mild viral encephalitis. Finally, we identified potential factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE using univariate analysis. The ultimate goal is to provide preliminary regional data that may help clinicians recognize SVE early and guide risk stratification, while acknowledging the exploratory nature of the findings.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionViral encephalitis is one of the most common central nervous system (CNS) infectious diseases in children. The disease progresses rapidly with diverse manifestations; severe cases often have poor outcomes (1). The incidence of viral encephalitis in children is significantly higher than in adults. Based on data from Henan Province during 2012–2023, approximately 4.5% of pediatric viral encephalitis cases progress to severe viral encephalitis (SVE), which was defined in that study as cases requiring pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission or presenting with altered consciousness or status epilepticus (2). SVE is characterized by acute onset, rapid progression, and high mortality (up to 8.4%) (3); some patients may evolve into acute necrotizing encephalopathy (4). Among survivors, about 20%–50% suffer from severe neurological sequelae (5), such as epilepsy, cognitive impairment, motor dysfunction, and behavioral abnormalities, which impose a long-term and heavy economic and psychological burden on families and society. Similar findings were reported by Gupta et al. in a retrospective study of pediatric acute encephalitis syndrome from eastern Uttar Pradesh, India, where a substantial proportion of survivors experienced long-term disability, including motor impairment and cognitive deficits (6). Qun Li et al. found that the incidence of sequelae, the number of patients receiving ICU treatment, and the number of deaths in the severe VE group were all significantly higher than those in the mild VE group (7). At present, the diagnosis of pediatric SVE mainly relies on clinical manifestations, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, and neuroimaging (8), but these methods have certain limitations. Therefore, early identification of SVE and understanding of exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality are crucial for timely and aggressive treatment. In the present study, we analyzed the clinical characteristics and ancillary examination findings of children with SVE to identify potential exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality using univariate analyses (with Firth-penalized-likelihood estimation to address complete separation), with the aim of improving clinicians’ understanding of pediatric SVE and reducing SVE-related mortality and disability. 2.1.Study subjectsAll cases were derived from pediatric inpatients diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital from January 2023 to December 2025. All enrolled children fulfilled comprehensive diagnostic criteria for viral encephalitis as follows: (1) Acute onset of neurological symptoms and signs; (2) CSF examination showing an elevated WBC count (> 10 × 106/L) with a predominance of lymphocytes, and/or a mild increase in protein; (3) Electroencephalogram and/or cranial imaging showing changes consistent with viral encephalitis; (4) Other central nervous system diseases such as purulent meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and autoimmune encephalitis were excluded. Alternative central nervous system infections were excluded according to the following criteria: 1) Bacterial purulent meningitis: excluded based on CSF profiles (predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes, low glucose, elevated protein), negative bacterial culture, and absence of clinical response to empirical antibiotic therapy. 2) Tuberculous meningitis: Excluded by CSF findings (lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein, decreased glucose), negative Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and clinical response to antiviral therapy rather than anti-tuberculous therapy. 3) Cryptococcal meningitis: Excluded by negative India ink stain and negative cryptococcal antigen test in CSF. 4) Autoimmune encephalitis: Excluded by negative testing for anti-neuronal antibodies (anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2, anti-GAD) in both serum and CSF.In terms of pathogen detection, all children provided blood and CSF samples that were tested using multiplex PCR method or serum virus IgM antibody detection to detect viruses: herpes simplex virus 1/2 type, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), human herpesvirus 6 type; at the same time, throat swabs were collected for respiratory virus PCR detection (including influenza virus A/B, human parainfluenza virus, SARS-CoV-2). Pathogen detection in CSF and blood was performed using the Multiplex PCR Kit (Anhui Ranchi Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China), which detects HSV-1/2, VZV, and HHV-6. Respiratory viruses were detected from throat swabs using the Respiratory Virus PCR Kit (Guojun Group Anqing Co., Ltd., China), which includes influenza A/B, human parainfluenza virus, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and SARS-CoV-2. Serum virus-specific IgM antibodies were measured using commercial ELISA kits (Hefei Anmeson Medical Devices Co., Ltd., China). Notably, pathogen detection rates are influenced by multiple factors, including sampling timing, viral load, and primer design. A negative pathogen assay result does not exclude a clinical diagnosis of viral encephalitis (9). In cases where pathogen testing was negative, a clinical diagnosis of viral encephalitis was accepted based on the comprehensive criteria described above (acute neurological symptoms, CSF pleocytosis with lymphocytic predominance, compatible EEG/neuroimaging findings, and exclusion of other CNS diseases).The patients were divided into two groups: a mild viral encephalitis group (n = 50) and an SVE group (n = 25). All patients met the diagnostic criteria for pediatric severe viral encephalitis as defined by a practical review on diagnostic approach and treatment. The diagnostic criteria for mild viral encephalitis were based on reference (10): All of the following clinical features must be met: 1) Consciousness state: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≥ 13 points (drowsy or agitated, but able to be awakened, and able to follow commands); 2) Seizure episodes: No seizures, or only single, brief convulsive episodes; 3) Focal signs: No obvious limb paralysis, cranial nerve palsy, or ataxia (or extremely mild and short-term recovery); 4) Intracranial hypertension: No severe headache, projectile vomiting, papilledema, and normal fundus examination; 5) Vital signs: Stable respiration, heart rate, and blood pressure, no need for ventilator support; 6) Daily abilities: Can eat independently, with basic life skills retained. The diagnostic criteria for SVE were adopted without modification from reference (7) and included at least one of the following conditions: (1) Frequent convulsions or status epilepticus; (2) Consciousness disturbance with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 8; (3) Limb paralysis or neurobehavioral abnormalities; (4) Brainstem symptoms; (5) Severe or persistent intracranial hypertension; (6) Multiple organ impairment progressing to failure. Because seizures and low GCS are components of the SVE definition, their associations with mortality within the SVE subgroup should be interpreted as severity markers rather than independent predictors. This study was approved by the ethics committee of Anqing Municipal Hospital (2024-94).Grouping based on GCS and seizures introduces definition-dependent differences between mild and severe cases; thus, comparisons serve only to describe clinical profiles, not to validate diagnostic values. In the prognostic regression analysis, whose primary outcome is in-hospital mortality within the SVE group, these variables are included as potential exploratory factors. However, because seizures and low GCS are components of the SVE definition, their association with mortality should be interpreted with caution, as discussed in the discussion section. Discharge-level functional prognosis was evaluated using the Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS): 1 = death, 2 = persistent vegetative state, 3 = severe disability, 4 = moderate disability, 5 = good recovery. title: Size, cytopathic effects, and prevalence of Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV in healthcare settings
abstract: Airborne transmission of respiratory viruses in healthcare settings is difficult to assess, particularly with respect to the size and viability of virus-containing aerosols. Most field studies rely on molecular detection, which limits inference about the infectiousness of virus. In this study we collected size-resolved airborne samples in a dental clinic and hospital during the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season using a BC (BioCascade)-BioSpot VIVAS (Viable Virus Aerosol Sampler). We analyzed these samples by RT-PCR and culture-based assays for influenza A, influenza B, SARS-CoV-2, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Viral RNA was detected in 11.1% of the 81 sampling events, with the highest positivity (25%) observed in pulmonary unit patient rooms. When influenza and SARS-CoV-2 RNA were detected, all of these detections occurred in the 4-10 μm size fraction, whereas all RSV RNA was detected in the <1.5 μm size fraction. Cell culture assays confirmed the presence of viable influenza in the samples that were positive by RT-PCR. Plaques were only observed for influenza A viral positive samples at the ‘neat’ or undiluted rate, whereas RSV and SARS-CoV-2 did not produce cytopathic effects in the cell culture assays. These findings highlight virus-specific differences in aerosol size distributions and the challenges of recovering viable virus from field-collected bioaerosols in healthcare environments.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to assess airborne transmission of respiratory viruses in healthcare settings, focusing on the size and viability of virus-containing aerosols. Airborne samples were collected in a dental clinic and hospital during the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season using a BC-BioSpot VIVAS sampler. Viral RNA was detected in 11.1% of 81 sampling events, with the highest positivity in pulmonary unit patient rooms. RSV RNA was consistently found in the <1.5 μm size fraction, while influenza and SARS-CoV-2 RNA were detected in the 4-10 μm size fraction. Cell culture assays confirmed the presence of viable influenza in RT-PCR-positive samples, but no cytopathic effects were observed for RSV or SARS-CoV-2. These results emphasize virus-specific differences in aerosol size distributions and the challenges of recovering viable virus from field samples. The study provides insights into the behavior of RSV in healthcare environments but does not address limitations or evidence strength.

abstract_zh: 在医疗保健环境中评估呼吸道病毒气溶胶的传播性(传播)具有挑战性,尤其是在病毒气溶胶的大小和活性方面。大多数现场研究依赖于分子检测,这限制了对病毒传染性的推断。本研究在2024-2025年呼吸道病毒季节期间,使用BC(BioCascade)-BioSpot VIVAS(可培养病毒气溶胶采样器)在牙科诊所和医院中收集了具有粒径分辨率的空气样本。我们通过RT-PCR和基于培养的检测方法分析了这些样本,以检测流感A型、流感B型、SARS-CoV-2和呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)。在81次采样事件中,有11.1%的样本检测到病毒RNA,其中肺病单元病房的阳性率最高(25%)。当检测到流感和SARS-CoV-2的RNA时,所有检测均发生在4-10 μm粒径组分中,而所有RSV RNA均检测到在<1.5 μm粒径组分中。细胞培养检测证实了通过RT-PCR检测为阳性的样本中存在可培养的流感病毒。仅在流感A型病毒阳性样本中观察到斑块,而RSV和SARS-CoV-2在细胞培养检测中未产生细胞病变效应。这些发现突显了不同病毒在气溶胶粒径分布上的特异性差异,以及在医疗保健环境中从现场收集的生物气溶胶中回收活性病毒的挑战。

title: Hyperinflammation and immunomodulation in influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and syncytial respiratory virus infection in adults: from innate immune responses and biomarkers to clinical and therapeutic implications

source_records.title: Hyperinflammation and immunomodulation in influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and syncytial respiratory virus infection in adults: from innate immune responses and biomarkers to clinical and therapeutic implications

full_text: AbstractInfluenza, SARS-CoV2-2 and syncytial respiratory virus infection in adults are major causes of morbidity and mortality. However, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying these infections remain incompletely understood. Disease severity results from an interaction between viral factors and host responses. Lung damage and respiratory failure are produced by hyperinflammation. Understanding these mechanisms is necessary to improve risk stratification and may guide therapeutic decisions. C- reactive protein (CRP), IL-6, ferritin, and ApoH are relevant biomarkers which can identify inflammatory phenotypes. Antivirals and supportive care are the main approaches for these viral infections. From a therapeutic perspective, broad immunosuppression is unlikely to be optimal, and strategies should focus on selectively modulating harmful inflammation while preserving antiviral immunity. Nevertheless, there is scarce evidence of the best choice of treatment based on the patient’s clinical profile and further studies are needed.Keywords: COVID-19, cytokine, IL-1, IL-6, immunomodulation, influenza, JAK inhibitors, respiratory syncytial virus 2.MethodsWe have designed a narrative review. A literature search was performed in the MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE and Cochrane Library databases without date restrictions. The search strategy included Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms. The MeSH words used were: “Influenza, Human,” “COVID-19,” “SARS-CoV-2,” “Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections,” “Immunity, Innate,” “Inflammation,” “Cytokines,” “Interleukin-6,” “Interleukine-1,” “Interferons,” “Biomarkers,” “Ferritins,” “Anti-Inflammatory Agents,” “Janus Kinase Inhibitors,” “Respiratory Distress Syndrome,” together with the free-text terms “hyperinflammation,” “respiratory viral infections,” “innate immunity,” “biomarkers,” “immunomodulatory therapies,” “cytokine storm,” “immune dysregulation,” “immunomodulation,” “NETosis,” “PTX3,” and “ApoH,” with a particular focus on influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV.Only articles published in English were included. Original research articles, randomized controlled trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant clinical practice guidelines were eligible for inclusion. References were selected based on their scientific quality, clinical relevance, and contribution to the objectives of this review.The literature was independently reviewed by three infectious disease specialists who selected the most relevant studies according to its quality, clinical relevance and contribution to the objectives of the review. The discrepancies were resolved through consensus among the three reviewers. Given the narrative nature of this work, no formal systematic review methodology, risk of bias assessment, or quantitative evidence synthesis was performed. This review primarily focuses on respiratory viral infections in adults. However, chosen pediatric studies were included, particularly in the context of RSV infection if no data was available for adults. 4.DiscussionThis review highlights that the clinical severity of SARS-CoV-2, Influenza and RSV is not only determined by viral replication. It also depends on the host early innate immune response. While early antiviral mechanisms are essential for pathogen clearance, hyperinflammation is determinant in lung injury, respiratory failure, and adverse outcomes.A central concept from this work is the balance between effective antiviral defense and the risk of immunopathology. Pro-inflammatory cytokine production and interferon signaling, play a critical role during the early phase of infection. However, these responses may be amplified and persist over time and contribute to tissue damage. This can lead to cytokine storm, inflammasome activation, and NETosis. This dual nature is exemplified by mediators such as IL-6, IL-1, TNF-α, and type I interferons, which are essential for host defense under controlled conditions but may become harmful when their regulation is lost.The identification of reliable biomarkers represents a critical step toward improving risk stratification and guiding therapeutic interventions. Among these, ferritin and IL-6 have emerged as indicators of hyperinflammation and disease severity. Ferritin is a potential mediator of inflammation, that self-amplifies inflammatory loop. Similarly, IL-6 reflects both immune activation and disease progression, although its dual role complicates its interpretation as a purely pathogenic factor. New molecules like ApoH have also been related to disease severity and immune dysregulation. Moreover, PTX3 is a new biomarker which is appropriated only for research settings and further studies are needed.As it has been discussed, these findings suggest that broad immunosuppression is unlikely to be the optimal approach. Instead, strategies should focus on selectively modulate harmful inflammation and preserve antiviral immunity. This concept is supported by the heterogeneous results observed with different immunomodulatory agents. Corticosteroids have shown benefit in selected conditions such as severe COVID-19 and septic shock but have shown inconsistent or potentially harmful effects in influenza and limited evidence in RSV. Similarly, targeted therapies against IL-6, IL-1, and JAK–STAT pathways have shown variable efficacy, often influenced by patient selection and timing of administration. Treatments during the early viral phase may impair antiviral responses, whereas treatment during the hyperinflammatory phase may stop tissue damage and improve outcomes. However, when it is administered too late, once organ damage has become established, they may have no effect.The integration of host-related factors, biomarkers of inflammation, and disease severity may contribute to improved risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making. In influenza, IL-6 and ferritin have shown prognostic value, but there is not a certain role guiding immunomodulatory treatment remains uncertain. It includes different study designs, patient populations, disease severity, therapeutic strategies, and outcome definitions, which limit direct comparisons across studies. Most evidence comes from observational studies or preclinical models. In particular, infectious complications have been poorly characterized in the available studies. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractInfluenza, SARS-CoV2-2 and syncytial respiratory virus infection in adults are major causes of morbidity and mortality. However, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying these infections remain incompletely understood. Disease severity results from an interaction between viral factors and host responses. Lung damage and respiratory failure are produced by hyperinflammation. Understanding these mechanisms is necessary to improve risk stratification and may guide therapeutic decisions. C- reactive protein (CRP), IL-6, ferritin, and ApoH are relevant biomarkers which can identify inflammatory phenotypes. Antivirals and supportive care are the main approaches for these viral infections. From a therapeutic perspective, broad immunosuppression is unlikely to be optimal, and strategies should focus on selectively modulating harmful inflammation while preserving antiviral immunity. Nevertheless, there is scarce evidence of the best choice of treatment based on the patient’s clinical profile and further studies are needed.Keywords: COVID-19, cytokine, IL-1, IL-6, immunomodulation, influenza, JAK inhibitors, respiratory syncytial virus
full_text_sections.methods: 2.MethodsWe have designed a narrative review. A literature search was performed in the MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE and Cochrane Library databases without date restrictions. The search strategy included Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms. The MeSH words used were: “Influenza, Human,” “COVID-19,” “SARS-CoV-2,” “Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections,” “Immunity, Innate,” “Inflammation,” “Cytokines,” “Interleukin-6,” “Interleukine-1,” “Interferons,” “Biomarkers,” “Ferritins,” “Anti-Inflammatory Agents,” “Janus Kinase Inhibitors,” “Respiratory Distress Syndrome,” together with the free-text terms “hyperinflammation,” “respiratory viral infections,” “innate immunity,” “biomarkers,” “immunomodulatory therapies,” “cytokine storm,” “immune dysregulation,” “immunomodulation,” “NETosis,” “PTX3,” and “ApoH,” with a particular focus on influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV.Only articles published in English were included. Original research articles, randomized controlled trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant clinical practice guidelines were eligible for inclusion. References were selected based on their scientific quality, clinical relevance, and contribution to the objectives of this review.The literature was independently reviewed by three infectious disease specialists who selected the most relevant studies according to its quality, clinical relevance and contribution to the objectives of the review. The discrepancies were resolved through consensus among the three reviewers. Given the narrative nature of this work, no formal systematic review methodology, risk of bias assessment, or quantitative evidence synthesis was performed. This review primarily focuses on respiratory viral infections in adults. However, chosen pediatric studies were included, particularly in the context of RSV infection if no data was available for adults.
