Similarly, IL-6 reflects both immune activation and disease progression, although its dual role complicates its interpretation as a purely pathogenic factor. New molecules like ApoH have also been related to disease severity and immune dysregulation. Moreover, PTX3 is a new biomarker which is appropriated only for research settings and further studies are needed.As it has been discussed, these findings suggest that broad immunosuppression is unlikely to be the optimal approach. Instead, strategies should focus on selectively modulate harmful inflammation and preserve antiviral immunity. This concept is supported by the heterogeneous results observed with different immunomodulatory agents. Corticosteroids have shown benefit in selected conditions such as severe COVID-19 and septic shock but have shown inconsistent or potentially harmful effects in influenza and limited evidence in RSV. full_text: AbstractRespiratory viral infections are increasingly recognized as important drivers of persistent airway symptoms and exacerbations in chronic lung disease. Post-infectious cough (PIC), particularly after upper respiratory tract infection, represents one of the most frequent causes of subacute cough and a mechanistically complex sequela in which cough hypersensitivity syndrome (CHS) plays a central pathophysiological role. Beyond increased cough frequency, patients with PIC frequently exhibit laryngeal sensory abnormalities and exaggerated responses to low-intensity stimuli, suggesting a sustained reduction in the activation threshold of airway sensory nerves. Among several contributors to cough hypersensitivity, P2X3 receptors and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are key ion-channel targets mediating cough reflexes and sensory nerve hypersensitivity, yet their clinical translation has been heterogeneous. Gefapixant reduced objective cough frequency in phase III trials enrolling refractory or unexplained chronic cough populations, but these data provide indirect rather than PIC-specific evidence, and its clinical utility is limited by dysgeusia. Similarly, TRPV1 antagonists suppress capsaicin-provoked cough but have not consistently improved spontaneous cough frequency, highlighting a disconnect between provocation models and real-world post-infectious cough pathology. This review discusses how respiratory viruses may induce cough hypersensitivity through transcriptional, metabolic, and neuroimmune regulation of sensory pathways. Respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and other viral pathogens can upregulate TRPV1, TRPA1, and ASIC3 expression, while cytokines such as IFN-γ may promote sensory-neuron transcriptional reprogramming through JAK-STAT and NF-κB signaling. In parallel, inflammatory mediators including bradykinin, COX/12-LOX metabolites, and prostaglandin E2 can sensitize TRP channels through kinase-dependent phosphorylation, whereas virus-induced epithelial ATP release and impaired CD39/CD73-mediated purinergic degradation may sustain repeated P2X3 receptor activation. Persistent peripheral afferent input may further induce central sensitization, explaining residual cough despite peripheral target blockade. By integrating viral immunopathogenesis, epithelial–neural crosstalk, and ion-channel pharmacology, this review proposes a framework for understanding post-viral cough hypersensitivity as a neuroimmune sequela of respiratory infection. Future research should prioritize molecular endotype-based stratification, PIC-specific randomized controlled trials, optimization of highly selective P2X3 antagonists, and combined peripheral–central assessment strategies to guide more precise therapeutic interventions.Keywords: cough hypersensitivity syndrome, P2X3 receptor, P2X3/TRP, post-infectious cough, TRP channels 6.4.Direct transcriptomic data from sensory neurons of human PIC patients remain absentAlthough virus-induced transcriptional alterations and sensory nerve plasticity have a plausible mechanistic basis, currently available direct evidence derives primarily from in vitro models, animal models, or indirect clinical observations (Dunne et al., 2025). Single-cell transcriptomic, spatial transcriptomic, or proteomic data from airway sensory neurons of human PIC patients are still lacking. Given the difficulty of obtaining tissues such as the nodose ganglion and jugular ganglion from patients, such research faces substantial technical and ethical constraints.Future studies may consider utilizing induced pluripotent stem cell-derived sensory neurons, airway epithelial-neuron co-cultures, organoid models, peripheral blood inflammatory markers, and non-invasive neuroimaging markers to establish a translatable research framework. Simultaneously, data on symptoms, cough frequency, channel provocation tests, inflammatory mediators, and metabolomics should be collected in prospective cohorts before and after infection to identify molecular features associated with PIC onset, persistence, and treatment response. Only through patient-level validation of these features can the transcriptional regulation framework be translated into clinical subtyping tools. 8.1.PIC patients with different predominant pathways require distinct targeted strategiesAvailable evidence indicates that treatment of PIC and chronic cough needs to transition from symptom-based empirical therapy toward precision stratification based on molecular endotypes. For patients characterized primarily by increased ATP release, insufficient ATP degradation, or enhanced P2X3 expression and function, P2X3 antagonists may offer greater therapeutic specificity. For patients in whom exogenous stimulus-triggered cough predominates, with elevated TRPV1 or TRPA1 provocation sensitivity, TRP-related pathways may carry greater pathological weight; however, whether TRPV1 blockade alone is sufficient remains uncertain. For patients with persistently elevated inflammatory mediators or abnormal metabolic microenvironments, anti-inflammatory therapy, neurogenic inflammation modulation, or metabolic interventions may serve as necessary adjuncts. Although P2X3 and TRP channels are the focus of this review, cough persistence may also be influenced by non-ion-channel contributors, including airway remodeling, microbiome alterations, autonomic dysfunction, and behavioral cough components. These mechanisms may interact with sensory hypersensitivity and should be considered in future PIC phenotyping studies.Achieving such stratified therapy requires clinically feasible and validated biomarkers (Table 3). The RCC/UCC field, which overlaps with but is not identical to PIC, currently lacks validated diagnostic or treatment-response predictive markers (Hassan et al., 2025). Near-term clinically feasible markers include objective cough frequency, validated cough-related quality-of-life scores, laryngeal sensory abnormality scores, and standardized capsaicin/ATP/AITC provocation sensitivity. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractRespiratory viral infections are increasingly recognized as important drivers of persistent airway symptoms and exacerbations in chronic lung disease. Post-infectious cough (PIC), particularly after upper respiratory tract infection, represents one of the most frequent causes of subacute cough and a mechanistically complex sequela in which cough hypersensitivity syndrome (CHS) plays a central pathophysiological role. Beyond increased cough frequency, patients with PIC frequently exhibit laryngeal sensory abnormalities and exaggerated responses to low-intensity stimuli, suggesting a sustained reduction in the activation threshold of airway sensory nerves. Among several contributors to cough hypersensitivity, P2X3 receptors and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are key ion-channel targets mediating cough reflexes and sensory nerve hypersensitivity, yet their clinical translation has been heterogeneous. Gefapixant reduced objective cough frequency in phase III trials enrolling refractory or unexplained chronic cough populations, but these data provide indirect rather than PIC-specific evidence, and its clinical utility is limited by dysgeusia. Similarly, TRPV1 antagonists suppress capsaicin-provoked cough but have not consistently improved spontaneous cough frequency, highlighting a disconnect between provocation models and real-world post-infectious cough pathology. This review discusses how respiratory viruses may induce cough hypersensitivity through transcriptional, metabolic, and neuroimmune regulation of sensory pathways. Respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and other viral pathogens can upregulate TRPV1, TRPA1, and ASIC3 expression, while cytokines such as IFN-γ may promote sensory-neuron transcriptional reprogramming through JAK-STAT and NF-κB signaling. In parallel, inflammatory mediators including bradykinin, COX/12-LOX metabolites, and prostaglandin E2 can sensitize TRP channels through kinase-dependent phosphorylation, whereas virus-induced epithelial ATP release and impaired CD39/CD73-mediated purinergic degradation may sustain repeated P2X3 receptor activation. Persistent peripheral afferent input may further induce central sensitization, explaining residual cough despite peripheral target blockade. By integrating viral immunopathogenesis, epithelial–neural crosstalk, and ion-channel pharmacology, this review proposes a framework for understanding post-viral cough hypersensitivity as a neuroimmune sequela of respiratory infection. Future research should prioritize molecular endotype-based stratification, PIC-specific randomized controlled trials, optimization of highly selective P2X3 antagonists, and combined peripheral–central assessment strategies to guide more precise therapeutic interventions.Keywords: cough hypersensitivity syndrome, P2X3 receptor, P2X3/TRP, post-infectious cough, TRP channels

Single-cell transcriptomic, spatial transcriptomic, or proteomic data from airway sensory neurons of human PIC patients are still lacking. For patients characterized primarily by increased ATP release, insufficient ATP degradation, or enhanced P2X3 expression and function, P2X3 antagonists may offer greater therapeutic specificity. For patients in whom exogenous stimulus-triggered cough predominates, with elevated TRPV1 or TRPA1 provocation sensitivity, TRP-related pathways may carry greater pathological weight; however, whether TRPV1 blockade alone is sufficient remains uncertain. full_text: THE OPENING of the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Congress 2026 placed patient partnership, equitable care, sustainability, and science-led policy at the centre of the respiratory agenda. The Congress opened in Barcelona, Spain, under the theme ‘Patient–Professional Partnership: United for Better Breathing’. The opening programme considered how lived experience can shape clinical decisions, research priorities, education, and public policy, while also highlighting digital care, health inequalities, planetary health, and the future respiratory workforce. CARE DESIGNED WITH PATIENTS Patient contributors called for care to be built with patients rather than simply delivered to them. Clinical expertise remains essential, but symptoms, treatment burden, emotional wellbeing, daily goals, and quality of life determine whether care works for the person receiving it. This requires shared decision-making based on trust and open discussion, with clinicians asking what matters in a patient’s everyday life. The programme reflected this commitment through 32 sessions with patient and professional co-chairs, 12 patient testimonials, and 46 patient speakers or panellists. Patient participation covered approximately one-quarter of the programme, including sessions on stigma, communication, service design, and patient contributions to ERS projects. SCIENCE CONNECTED TO EVERYDAY CARE Organisers reported just under 7,200 abstract submissions, the highest number received by the Congress. Programme highlights included new respiratory pharmacotherapies, treatment escalation following a COPD exacerbation, inhaler technology, and digital applications. Sessions also explored equity in respiratory care, transitions from paediatric to adult services, and communication between patients, parents, and clinicians. Environmental and geopolitical pressures also featured. Planned discussions addressed net zero respiratory healthcare, the effects of food systems and lifestyle on respiratory health, and the disruption of care during conflict. RESEARCH EDUCATION AND ADVOCACY ERS outlined work with the European Lung Foundation (ELF) on a research strategy incorporating the priorities of HCPs and patients. It also highlighted international scientific collaboration and initiatives supporting medical students, allied HCPs, and basic scientists entering respiratory careers. Digital and on-demand education is intended to improve access for a membership in which around one-third of members are based outside Europe. Advocacy leaders also identified tobacco and nicotine use, air pollution, climate change, occupational exposures, and respiratory infections as priorities requiring evidence-based policy. PARTNERSHIP BEYOND THE CONGRESS The opening programme presented patient partnership as a working method rather than a ceremonial theme. Its success will depend on whether patients continue to shape routine care, research questions, education, and policy after delegates leave Barcelona. Residual T2 Inflammation Linked to Severe Asthma Relapse APPROXIMATELY one in five patients with severe asthma who achieved clinical remission after starting biologic therapy experienced relapse during the following year, according to an international registry study presented at ERS 2026.1 Researchers used data from the International Severe Asthma Registry (ISAR) to identify factors associated with relapse among adults who had at least 2 consecutive years of follow-up. All included patients had achieved clinical remission 12 months after initiating biologic treatment. Clinical remission was defined using three criteria: no exacerbations, no long-term oral corticosteroid use, and partly or well-controlled asthma. Relapse was recorded when a patient no longer met at least one of these criteria at 24 months. Among 732 patients from 21 countries who were in remission at 12 months, 148 patients, or 20.2%, had relapsed by 24 months. Better lung function was associated with a lower likelihood of relapse. Patients with a percent predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 second of at least 80% had 38% lower odds of relapse than those with values below 80%. Markers of persistent Type 2 inflammation were associated with poorer remission durability. Patients with a blood eosinophil count of at least 100 cells/μL had approximately twice the odds of relapse compared with those with counts below 50 cells/μL. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide measured at 12 months was not independently associated with relapse. However, patients whose levels had fallen by less than 34% between the pre-biologic assessment and 12 months had higher odds of relapse than those with reductions of at least 34%. These findings suggest that most patients who achieve remission with biologic treatment maintain it for at least another year. However, residual Type 2 inflammation and reduced lung function at 12 months may help identify patients requiring closer monitoring. As an observational analysis, the study identifies associations and does not establish that these factors directly cause relapse. Functional Capacity May Explain Sex Differences After Lung Surger MEN undergoing lung cancer surgery may have higher postoperative risk than women, with differences in functional capacity potentially accounting for much of this association, according to findings presented at ERS 2026.2 Findings suggest that differences in preoperative functional capacity may help explain sex-related differences in outcomes following lung cancer surgery. Sex differences in postoperative outcomes are well documented, but the role of functional capacity in determining surgical selection and subsequent risk remains less clear. The study investigated whether differences in cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) performance could help explain these differences. Researchers assessed 498 patients referred for CPET between 2008–2020 and reviewed the reasons why patients did not proceed to surgical treatment. CPET measures included weight-indexed peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), percent-predicted VO2peak, and the ventilatory equivalent for carbon dioxide (VE/VCO2) slope. Logistic regression was used to examine whether sex was associated with major pulmonary complications or 30-day mortality among patients undergoing lobectomy, with sequential adjustment for comorbidities, surgical factors, and CPET-derived variables. Of the patients assessed, 224 underwent resection, including 149 who underwent lobectomy. Women who were excluded from surgery had relatively preserved functional capacity. Their mean percent-predicted VO2peak was 80%, while the mean VE/VCO2 slope was 35.8. These measures were comparable with those seen in men who subsequently underwent lobectomy, whose corresponding values were 78% and 35.1. Among patients undergoing lobectomy, male sex was initially associated with an increased risk of major pulmonary complications or 30-day mortality, with an odds ratio (OR) of 3.15 and a 95% CI of 1.39–7.16. This association remained after adjustment for comorbidities and surgical extent, with an OR of 2.69 and a 95% CI of 1.11–6.50. However, the association was no longer apparent after percent-predicted VO2peak was included in the analysis, when the OR was 1.39 with a 95% CI of 0.51–3.77. These findings suggest that differences in functional capacity may account for much of the observed sex-related variation in postoperative risk. They also raise questions about how CPET measures are incorporated into multidisciplinary decisions regarding lung cancer surgery, particularly where women with preserved exercise capacity may not proceed to resection. The observational nature of the study means that the findings cannot establish causality, and further research is required to determine how functional capacity should be incorporated into surgical decision-making. The authors suggest that percent-predicted VO2peak or VE/VCO2 slope may provide useful measures for assessing risk across sexes. Higher Levels of Growth Differentiation Factor 15 in Patients with Asthma Suggests Role in Pathogenesis GROWTH differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15) may play a role in asthma pathogenesis after a new study presented at ERS 2026 revealed that circulating GDF-15 levels are higher in patients with asthma and continue to be linked to fixed airway obstruction and asthma exacerbation rate.3 Asthma is known to be related to an increased risk of developing certain thromboembolic complications, while GDF-15, a multifunctional cytokine that has anti-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic properties, is linked to cardiovascular risk. This study looked at the relationship between concentrations of GDF-15 in the peripheral blood of patients with asthma and their relationship with asthma severity, lung function, exacerbation rate, and a set of inflammatory and prothrombotic biomarkers. In total, 157 adult patients with asthma were matched with 60 controls. Plasma GDF-15 was determined in relation to a number of factors including inflammatory and prothrombotic markers, such as thrombin generation profile, fibrinolysis (measured by clot lysis time [CLT]), and cellular fibronectin. During the 3-year follow-up period of this study, researchers also assessed the asthma exacerbation rate. The results showed that GDF-15 levels were 10.8% higher in patients with asthma (p<0.001). Moreover, GDF-15 levels positively correlated with longer CLT, implying impaired fibrinolysis (Pearson correlation coefficient [r]=0.39; p<0.001), cellular fibronectin (r=0.37; p<0.001), and C-reactive protein (r=0.18; p=0.025). Conversely, higher GDF-15 levels were not correlated with thrombin generation parameters. Baseline GDF-15 levels were 13.9% higher in patients with fixed airway obstruction (p=0.024). However, these baseline levels were not associated with asthma severity or forced expiratory volume in 1 second. Interestingly, researchers also recorded 150 severe asthma exacerbations in 50 patients. These individuals exhibited 12.3% higher GDF-15 at baseline (p=0.003). Overall, the findings indicate that patients with asthma have higher circulating GDF-15 levels and that they remain associated with fixed airway obstruction and asthma exacerbation rate. The authors explained that this study is the first to demonstrate higher GDF-15 levels in patients with asthma and, as a result, suggested that GDF-15 may play a role in asthma pathogenesis. Personalised Campaign Increases Influenza Vaccination Uptake in High-Risk Groups A PERSONALISED communication campaign delivered by a Slovak health insurance company (HIC) has been associated with increased influenza vaccination among high-risk individuals, according to a late-breaking abstract presented at ERS 2026.4 Influenza vaccination coverage in Slovakia has remained low, at 3.8% in the general population and between 1.9–15.5% among high-risk groups, representing an underused preventive opportunity. The study aimed to assess whether a personalised communication campaign delivered by a HIC was associated with increased influenza vaccination among high-risk individuals. An administrative database from a Slovak HIC, covering 1.8 million insurees in 2025, was used to identify high-risk individuals, including those with asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease, or diabetes; adults aged 59 years and over; and pregnant women. A personalised campaign was delivered via email, SMS, or push notification between October–November 2025. Vaccine prescriptions by the end of December 2025 were compared against 232,153 insurees who did not receive the campaign, using multivariable logistic regression. The campaign reached 232,159 high-risk individuals, of whom 13,679 (5.9%) filled a vaccine prescription. Personalised communication was associated with a 23% increase in odds of vaccination, corresponding to 1,853 additional vaccinations. Pregnant women showed the highest adjusted odds (odds ratio: 1.37), and patients with respiratory disease also had significantly higher odds (odds ratio: 1.21) versus the cardiovascular disease reference group. Prior-year vaccination was the strongest predictor, with up to 30-fold higher odds. SMS was less effective than email, with 8% lower odds of vaccination. The authors have concluded that HIC-led personalised communication represents a simple, effective, and scalable tool to support influenza vaccination uptake in high-risk populations. Lower Risk of Cardiovascular Events Associated with AS01E-Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 Vaccine IN ADULTS aged 60 years and over, the AS01E-adjuvanted respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein (RSVPreF3)-based vaccine was associated with a lower risk of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)-related major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and respiratory exacerbations over two RSV seasons, according to a retrospective cohort study presented at ERS 2026.5 Current research suggests that the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine is effective in reducing the risk of a number of RSV-related outcomes over one RSV season. These include reducing the risk of MACE, severe exacerbations of COPD, and asthma. However, in this study, researchers aimed to evaluate vaccine effectiveness (VE) over two RSV seasons. The study included 662,982 vaccinated and 2,651,928 unvaccinated adults in the USA aged 60 years and over, and was conducted using claims data obtained from the Optum Research Database. The claims data used spanned almost 3 years from August 2022–May 2025. Vaccinated and unvaccinated adults were exact matched on key baseline characteristics. Propensity score weighting was used to balance the remaining differences, and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios that compared the risk of overall and RSV-related MACE and COPD and asthma exacerbations. The median follow-up of vaccinated adults was 16.4 months, whereas the median follow-up of unvaccinated adults was 14.3 months. Against RSV-related outcomes, VE was 58.5% for MACE (95% CI: 46.0–68.1%). Regarding respiratory outcomes, VE was 57.6% for severe COPD exacerbations (95% CI: 46.1–66.7%), and 57.3% for severe asthma exacerbations (95% CI: 22.3–76.6%). Overall, this study revealed that in adults from the USA aged 60 years and over, adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccination was associated with a lower risk of RSV-related MACE, COPD exacerbations, and asthma exacerbations over two RSV seasons. The authors concluded by outlining the clinical implications of these findings. They suggested that the results may help inform future recommendations in revaccination timing. Aerosolised Budesonide/Formoterol Does Not Reduce Respiratory Failure in Hospitalised Pneumonia A LARGE multicentre RCT has found that aerosolised budesonide/formoterol does not significantly reduce acute respiratory failure in hospitalised patients with pneumonia and hypoxaemia, according to findings presented at ERS 2026.6 The Phase III ARREST trial enrolled 465 patients between May 2020–July 2025. Participants were randomly assigned to receive twice-daily aerosolised budesonide/formoterol or placebo for up to 5 days. The double-blind study excluded patients who already had an indication for inhaled beta agonists or corticosteroids, although the protocol was amended to permit 6 mg dexamethasone in patients with COVID-19. The primary endpoint was acute respiratory failure, defined as requiring high-flow nasal oxygen or non-invasive or invasive ventilation for more than 36 hours. Researchers also explored whether the treatment effect differed across prespecified patient subgroups. Acute respiratory failure occurred in 47 of 235 patients (20.0%) receiving budesonide/formoterol and 50 of 230 patients (21.7%) receiving placebo. This difference was not statistically significant (odds ratio: 0.9; 95% CI: 0.6–1.5; p=0.7), and no differences were observed in secondary outcomes. The median time from presentation to the emergency department to administration of the first dose was 20 hours. Subgroup analysis suggested a possible effect of treatment timing: patients treated within 20 hours showed a trend towards a lower risk of acute respiratory failure compared with those treated later. However, the interaction did not reach conventional statistical significance and should be interpreted cautiously. The trial was stopped for futility after reaching 75% of its planned enrolment, limiting its ability to identify smaller treatment effects. The timing of treatment initiation may also have influenced the results, while the protocol amendment permitting dexamethasone in patients with COVID-19 introduced potential variation in concomitant corticosteroid exposure. Overall, the findings do not support routine use of aerosolised budesonide/formoterol to prevent acute respiratory failure in hospitalised patients with pneumonia and hypoxaemia. Further research would be needed to determine whether earlier administration could benefit selected patients. full_text_sections.full_text: THE OPENING of the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Congress 2026 placed patient partnership, equitable care, sustainability, and science-led policy at the centre of the respiratory agenda. The Congress opened in Barcelona, Spain, under the theme ‘Patient–Professional Partnership: United for Better Breathing’. The opening programme considered how lived experience can shape clinical decisions, research priorities, education, and public policy, while also highlighting digital care, health inequalities, planetary health, and the future respiratory workforce. CARE DESIGNED WITH PATIENTS Patient contributors called for care to be built with patients rather than simply delivered to them. Clinical expertise remains essential, but symptoms, treatment burden, emotional wellbeing, daily goals, and quality of life determine whether care works for the person receiving it. This requires shared decision-making based on trust and open discussion, with clinicians asking what matters in a patient’s everyday life. The programme reflected this commitment through 32 sessions with patient and professional co-chairs, 12 patient testimonials, and 46 patient speakers or panellists. Patient participation covered approximately one-quarter of the programme, including sessions on stigma, communication, service design, and patient contributions to ERS projects. SCIENCE CONNECTED TO EVERYDAY CARE Organisers reported just under 7,200 abstract submissions, the highest number received by the Congress. Programme highlights included new respiratory pharmacotherapies, treatment escalation following a COPD exacerbation, inhaler technology, and digital applications. Sessions also explored equity in respiratory care, transitions from paediatric to adult services, and communication between patients, parents, and clinicians. Environmental and geopolitical pressures also featured. Planned discussions addressed net zero respiratory healthcare, the effects of food systems and lifestyle on respiratory health, and the disruption of care during conflict. RESEARCH EDUCATION AND ADVOCACY ERS outlined work with the European Lung Foundation (ELF) on a research strategy incorporating the priorities of HCPs and patients. It also highlighted international scientific collaboration and initiatives supporting medical students, allied HCPs, and basic scientists entering respiratory careers. Digital and on-demand education is intended to improve access for a membership in which around one-third of members are based outside Europe. Advocacy leaders also identified tobacco and nicotine use, air pollution, climate change, occupational exposures, and respiratory infections as priorities requiring evidence-based policy. PARTNERSHIP BEYOND THE CONGRESS The opening programme presented patient partnership as a working method rather than a ceremonial theme. Its success will depend on whether patients continue to shape routine care, research questions, education, and policy after delegates leave Barcelona. Residual T2 Inflammation Linked to Severe Asthma Relapse APPROXIMATELY one in five patients with severe asthma who achieved clinical remission after starting biologic therapy experienced relapse during the following year, according to an international registry study presented at ERS 2026.1 Researchers used data from the International Severe Asthma Registry (ISAR) to identify factors associated with relapse among adults who had at least 2 consecutive years of follow-up. All included patients had achieved clinical remission 12 months after initiating biologic treatment. Clinical remission was defined using three criteria: no exacerbations, no long-term oral corticosteroid use, and partly or well-controlled asthma. Relapse was recorded when a patient no longer met at least one of these criteria at 24 months. Among 732 patients from 21 countries who were in remission at 12 months, 148 patients, or 20.2%, had relapsed by 24 months. Better lung function was associated with a lower likelihood of relapse. Patients with a percent predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 second of at least 80% had 38% lower odds of relapse than those with values below 80%. Markers of persistent Type 2 inflammation were associated with poorer remission durability. Patients with a blood eosinophil count of at least 100 cells/μL had approximately twice the odds of relapse compared with those with counts below 50 cells/μL. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide measured at 12 months was not independently associated with relapse. However, patients whose levels had fallen by less than 34% between the pre-biologic assessment and 12 months had higher odds of relapse than those with reductions of at least 34%. These findings suggest that most patients who achieve remission with biologic treatment maintain it for at least another year. However, residual Type 2 inflammation and reduced lung function at 12 months may help identify patients requiring closer monitoring. As an observational analysis, the study identifies associations and does not establish that these factors directly cause relapse. full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02506-0 Comment Acute infection as a driver of chronic diseases and the unsung benefits of vaccination In Su Cheon, Mark T. Esser & Jie Sun Acute infections can leave durable biological imprints that alter host physiology, chronic disease susceptibility, long-term health and even biological ageing, well after pathogen clearance. Vaccines should therefore be evaluated not only on their ability to prevent acute illness, but also on their efficacy in preventing or mitigating these long-lasting biological imprints and infection-associated chronic conditions. From microbial exposure and symptom onset to clinical recovery, acute infection has traditionally been viewed as a temporary distur- bance of host physiology. This view has shaped clinical care, public health policy and vaccine evaluation. However, growing clinical and experimental evidence indicates that this view is increasingly outdated. Many pathogens can cause symptoms that persist well beyond clear- ance of the infectious agent. Long COVID, also known as post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection, is the best example and has raised public awareness of infection-associated chronic conditions and ill- nesses (IACCIs)1. It is estimated that at least 400 million individuals worldwide currently suffer from long COVID. The broad definition of long COVID describes a post-acute condition in which symptoms usually occur or persist 3 months after infection onset, last for at least 2 months, and cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis2. Com- mon symptoms include chronic fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog or exercise-intolerance. Long COVID demonstrates that, even after the acute phase has been resolved, infection can leave a persistent host state that impairs long-term quality of life. IACCI occurrence is not unique to SARS-CoV-2 infection and has been reported after other acute respiratory viral infections3. Systemic or local- ized infections have been associated with chronic illnesses that can last months to years, including group A Streptococcus, Lyme disease, influenza virus, Ebola virus, dengue and Epstein–Barr virus4. The lingering ‘tails’ of infectious disease can be generally understood as a failure to return fully to baseline after the initial illness. IACCIs often share a core series of common symptoms, including chronic fatigue, cognitive problems, sleep disorders and pain, while also displaying pathogen-specific heterogene- ity. Together, these syndromes establish an essential principle: the end of acute infection is not necessarily the end of the disease. More broadly, infections differ substantially in their long-term host legacy (see Box 1). Impacts on pre-existing chronic disease and the development of new chronic illness Acute infection can also alter the trajectory of chronic disease. By induc- ing injury, inflammation, tissue remodelling and systemic stress, acute infection can exacerbate or accelerate pre-existing chronic diseases and, in some settings, contribute to the initiation of new chronic ill- ness. For example, acute respiratory infections commonly exacerbate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Acute idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis exacerbations by infec- tions not only increase acute morbidity and mortality but can accel- erate the progression of fibrotic lung conditions and leave survivors with persistent loss of lung function. In this context, acute infection is not simply an added complication, but causes a stepwise injury and tissue remodelling that shifts patients onto a worse disease trajectory5. An even more provocative possibility is that acute infections can contribute to the development of new chronic diseases, including cancer. Large cohort studies have shown increased post-acute risks of chronic conditions including new onset of diabetes and autoimmun- ity development after SARS-CoV-2 infection6. Furthermore, elevated cardiovascular risk can persist for months, not only after infection with SARS-CoV-2, but also after influenza or respiratory syncytial virus infection, increasing in a graded fashion with acute disease severity6,7. Persistent or latent infections, such as human papillomavirus and hepatitis viruses, are well-established drivers of cancer development. However, emerging evidence suggests that even acute, non-persistent infections can influence cancer biology by reshaping tissue micro- environments after pathogen clearance. For instance, prior severe respiratory viral infection with SARS-CoV-2 or influenza was linked to accelerated lung cancer growth in mouse models and increased subsequent lung cancer risk among patients hospitalized for COVID-19 (ref. 8). In this context, severe viral injury potentially leaves behind a durable tissue, immune and epigenetic ‘scar’ that alters the local microenvironment, modifies future cancer risk and promotes tumour development under permissive conditions. Together, these observations support a model in which acute infection should be considered not only as an exacerbator of underly- ing chronic diseases, but as a potential cause of chronic diseases. This reframes the central clinical inquiry from a narrow focus on immedi- ate outcomes to a broader analysis of long-term consequences after acute infection. Addressing the latter question will require long-term clinical follow-up that extends well beyond the apparent acute recov- ery. In parallel, mechanistic studies are needed to determine how transient infectious events fundamentally and persistently rewire host epigenetic, molecular and cellular pathways across the body. Such clinical and scientific efforts will be essential for understanding how acute infections leave durable host imprints and for developing interventions that protect against not only acute illness, but also its long-term consequences. Acute infection can accelerate biological ageing Ageing is the most important risk factor for the development of many chronic diseases, including heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s dis- ease. Increasing evidence suggests that acute infections can accelerate Check for updates nature microbiology Comment features of biological ageing. Studies using DNA methylation-based epi- genetic clocks have revealed accelerated epigenetic age in patients with COVID-19, particularly in those with severe disease9. Beyond the acute phase, post-COVID-19 cohorts show persistent altered immune ageing10, suggesting that infection can leave a durable imprint in pro-ageing path- ways. Together, these studies support a model in which SARS-CoV-2 infection can shift the host towards an older biological state. Similar observations are emerging from other acute infections. Influenza virus infection can promote cellular senescence in the lung, and the depletion of senescent cells reduces persistent lung pathology and improves epithelial repair in mouse models11. These findings support a model in which acute infection can function as a stressor to enhance tissue senescence and ageing, which in turn drives post-infection tissue remodelling. Although definitive evidence is still currently lacking, acute infection may shift the host towards a state of premature biological ageing and shortened health span or even life span, by possibly engaging multiple hallmarks of ageing, including chronic inflammation, DNA damage, telomere attrition, epigenetic remodelling, cellular senescence and so on. Nevertheless, this may help explain why a single infectious insult can produce persistent, systemic or multi-organ chronic consequences long after pathogen clearance. Vaccine efficacy beyond acute infection If acute infections can cause post-acute syndromes, worsen chronic dis- ease, initiate new chronic illness and accelerate biological ageing, then anti-microbial agents and vaccines must confer benefits that extend far beyond the prevention of immediate illness. Yet most vaccine efficacy and effectiveness trials measure only short-term endpoints including infection, disease mitigation, and prevention of acute hospitalization and death. These outcomes are important but capture only the acute phase of host protection. Observational studies and meta-analyses indicate that vacci- nation before SARS-CoV-2 infection reduces the risk of long COVID. Notably, a nationwide French cohort of 28 million adults found that mRNA COVID-19-vaccinated individuals had lower all-cause mortal- ity over 4 years, strongly suggesting that COVID-19 vaccination ben- efited long-term health outcomes12. Similarly, the influenza vaccine is another well-documented example of an immunization that prevents the onset and exacerbation of deleterious chronic conditions, includ- ing cardiovascular events13. These findings highlight a limitation of most vaccine studies. A vaccine that does not fully provide sterilizing immunity (such as cur- rent COVID-19 vaccines or influenza vaccines) may still reduce viral burden, inflammatory amplification, organ damage and downstream chronic disease risk. Thus, the long-term benefit of vaccination may be substantial even when acute protection against infection appears incomplete or modest, as long as it ameliorates disease severity during the acute phase. In this sense, vaccines should be viewed not only as tools to prevent acute infectious disease, but also as disease-modifying interventions that may preserve long-term organ function, immune homeostasis, health span and survival. In a climate of vaccine fatigue and declining public trust, a more complete accounting of vaccine benefits is both scientifically necessary and socially urgent. The public are often told that vaccines prevent infection or acute illness. That is true, but incomplete. The underappreciated benefit of vaccination may be protection of the future health of the individual, particularly by reducing the lifetime burden of diseases that can be initiated or accelerated by an acute infection. BOX 1 The long-term host legacies of infection Infections may differ in their capacity to leave a durable imprint on host health. Recognizing which infections commonly carry a long-lasting host legacy, and those for which such effects have not been consistently demonstrated, could help identify where infection prevention may provide long-term benefits. Infections that leave a harmful legacy Examples of infections that lead to chronic sequelae, exacerbate pre-existing diseases, cause new chronic conditions or accelerate biological ageing4: SARS-CoV-2 (long COVID, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and accelerated ageing); influenza (long flu and cardiovascular conditions); respiratory syncytial virus (asthma risk and cardiovascular events); Epstein–Barr virus (multiple sclerosis and cancer); group A Streptococcus (rheumatic heart disease and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis); poliovirus (post-polio syndrome); measles (immune amnesia and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (post-tuberculosis lung disease); Borrelia burgdorferi (post-treatment Lyme syndrome); and Ebola (post-Ebola syndrome). No consistently established long-term legacy For some generally self-limited infections such as common cold coronavirus and adenovirus infections, durable population-level sequelae have not been systematically demonstrated. This category may reflect limited long-term follow-up rather than proof that such infections are harmless in the long run. Microbial exposures associated with potentially beneficial immune calibration Early life exposure to commensal microbiota and diverse environmental microorganisms may help to calibrate immune development15. The hygiene hypothesis proposes that reduced exposure to microorganisms with which humans co-evolved may contribute to increased allergic and autoimmune risk later in life. Certain helminth and microbial pathogen exposures (such as hookworm and Helicobacter pylori) have also been associated with immuno­ regulatory effects. Nevertheless, these organisms can themselves cause substantial morbidity and should not be considered as inherently beneficial. Live attenuated vaccines such as Bacillus Calmette–Guérin can induce trained innate immune responses and may provide heterologous protection in some settings without the pathological legacy of natural infection. nature microbiology Comment We therefore propose a two-axis framework for vaccine evaluation in the future (Fig. 1). The first axis measures acute protection, that is, what has already been implemented, such as infection rate, sympto- matic diseases, hospitalization and death. The second axis, which we view as important, measures chronic protection, including the preven- tion or attenuation of IACCIs, pre-existing condition exacerbation, new-onset chronic disease, accelerated biological ageing, health span loss and/or long-term mortality. Different vaccines may perform differ- ently across these parameters. Some may strongly prevent infection, while others may primarily reduce chronic sequelae of acute infection. We think that the protection of both acute and chronic illness matters and should be clearly communicated to the public. To implement this broader framework, vaccine trials and real-world effectiveness studies should include longer follow-up and, where possible, connect study participants to electronic health records and chronic disease registries so that later outcomes can be measured systematically. Such long-term tracking would not only clarify the full impact of vaccination on host health but also provide rigorous evidence to counter misinformation that vaccines cause long-term harm. These studies should also use standardized definitions for IACCIs and track outcomes that reflect long-term health, including new or worsening chronic diseases, and measures of biological ageing, frailty, functional decline and extended all-cause mortality. A practical limitation to this recommendation is cost. Imple- menting such studies could cost hundreds of millions of dollars if performed as a randomized controlled clinical trial. Registry-enabled pragmatic, randomized trials offer one approach to improve feasibility. For example, the DANFLU-2 trial randomized aged adults to high-dose or standard-dose inactivated influenza vaccine and used routinely collected health-registry data for outcome ascertainment. In the pre- specified FLUNITY-HD pooled analysis of DANFLU-2, high-dose vaccina- tion was associated with fewer hospitalizations for heart failure than standard-dose vaccination in an exploratory outcome analysis14. Public health and cost-effectiveness models should similarly include chronic disease burden when estimating the value of vaccination. In parallel, mechanistic studies are needed to determine how prior vaccination prevents or reduces the pathogen-driven and host inflammatory path- ways that lead to chronic disease, impaired tissue repair, accelerated biological ageing or decreased health and life span. Conclusion Acute infection should no longer be treated as a short-lived episode with only temporary consequences. It can be an origin point for long-term chronic disease, a modifier of chronic illness and a possible accelerator of biological ageing. Recognizing this chronic host legacy will reshape infection biology, chronic disease research and vaccine evaluation. The true burden of infection is therefore not limited to acute morbid- ity and mortality, but extends to the occurrence of chronic diseases, functional decline and biological ageing trajectories that may emerge months or years later. Likewise, the true value of vaccination should not be measured only by whether it prevents acute illness today, but also by whether it protects the future health of the individual. Esser & Jie Sun Acute infections can leave durable biological imprints that alter host physiology, chronic disease susceptibility, long-term health and even biological ageing, well after pathogen clearance. Vaccines should therefore be evaluated not only on their ability to prevent acute illness, but also on their efficacy in preventing or mitigating these long-lasting biological imprints and infection-associated chronic conditions. From microbial exposure and symptom onset to clinical recovery, acute infection has traditionally been viewed as a temporary distur- bance of host physiology. This view has shaped clinical care, public health policy and vaccine evaluation. However, growing clinical and experimental evidence indicates that this view is increasingly outdated. Many pathogens can cause symptoms that persist well beyond clear- ance of the infectious agent. Long COVID, also known as post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection, is the best example and has raised public awareness of infection-associated chronic conditions and ill- nesses (IACCIs)1. It is estimated that at least 400 million individuals worldwide currently suffer from long COVID. The broad definition of long COVID describes a post-acute condition in which symptoms usually occur or persist 3 months after infection onset, last for at least 2 months, and cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis2. Com- mon symptoms include chronic fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog or exercise-intolerance. Long COVID demonstrates that, even after the acute phase has been resolved, infection can leave a persistent host state that impairs long-term quality of life. IACCI occurrence is not unique to SARS-CoV-2 infection and has been reported after other acute respiratory viral infections3. Systemic or local- ized infections have been associated with chronic illnesses that can last months to years, including group A Streptococcus, Lyme disease, influenza virus, Ebola virus, dengue and Epstein–Barr virus4. The lingering ‘tails’ of infectious disease can be generally understood as a failure to return fully to baseline after the initial illness. IACCIs often share a core series of common symptoms, including chronic fatigue, cognitive problems, sleep disorders and pain, while also displaying pathogen-specific heterogene- ity. Together, these syndromes establish an essential principle: the end of acute infection is not necessarily the end of the disease. More broadly, infections differ substantially in their long-term host legacy (see Box 1). Impacts on pre-existing chronic disease and the development of new chronic illness Acute infection can also alter the trajectory of chronic disease. By induc- ing injury, inflammation, tissue remodelling and systemic stress, acute infection can exacerbate or accelerate pre-existing chronic diseases and, in some settings, contribute to the initiation of new chronic ill- ness. For example, acute respiratory infections commonly exacerbate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Acute idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis exacerbations by infec- tions not only increase acute morbidity and mortality but can accel- erate the progression of fibrotic lung conditions and leave survivors with persistent loss of lung function. In this context, acute infection is not simply an added complication, but causes a stepwise injury and tissue remodelling that shifts patients onto a worse disease trajectory5. An even more provocative possibility is that acute infections can contribute to the development of new chronic diseases, including cancer. Large cohort studies have shown increased post-acute risks of chronic conditions including new onset of diabetes and autoimmun- ity development after SARS-CoV-2 infection6. Furthermore, elevated cardiovascular risk can persist for months, not only after infection with SARS-CoV-2, but also after influenza or respiratory syncytial virus infection, increasing in a graded fashion with acute disease severity6,7. Persistent or latent infections, such as human papillomavirus and hepatitis viruses, are well-established drivers of cancer development. However, emerging evidence suggests that even acute, non-persistent infections can influence cancer biology by reshaping tissue micro- environments after pathogen clearance. For instance, prior severe respiratory viral infection with SARS-CoV-2 or influenza was linked to accelerated lung cancer growth in mouse models and increased subsequent lung cancer risk among patients hospitalized for COVID-19 (ref. 8). In this context, severe viral injury potentially leaves behind a durable tissue, immune and epigenetic ‘scar’ that alters the local microenvironment, modifies future cancer risk and promotes tumour development under permissive conditions. Together, these observations support a model in which acute infection should be considered not only as an exacerbator of underly- ing chronic diseases, but as a potential cause of chronic diseases. This reframes the central clinical inquiry from a narrow focus on immedi- ate outcomes to a broader analysis of long-term consequences after acute infection. Addressing the latter question will require long-term clinical follow-up that extends well beyond the apparent acute recov- ery. In parallel, mechanistic studies are needed to determine how transient infectious events fundamentally and persistently rewire host epigenetic, molecular and cellular pathways across the body. Such clinical and scientific efforts will be essential for understanding how acute infections leave durable host imprints and for developing interventions that protect against not only acute illness, but also its long-term consequences. Acute infection can accelerate biological ageing Ageing is the most important risk factor for the development of many chronic diseases, including heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s dis- ease. Increasing evidence suggests that acute infections can accelerate Check for updates nature microbiology Comment features of biological ageing. Studies using DNA methylation-based epi- genetic clocks have revealed accelerated epigenetic age in patients with COVID-19, particularly in those with severe disease9. Beyond the acute phase, post-COVID-19 cohorts show persistent altered immune ageing10, suggesting that infection can leave a durable imprint in pro-ageing path- ways. Together, these studies support a model in which SARS-CoV-2 infection can shift the host towards an older biological state. Similar observations are emerging from other acute infections. Influenza virus infection can promote cellular senescence in the lung, and the depletion of senescent cells reduces persistent lung pathology and improves epithelial repair in mouse models11. These findings support a model in which acute infection can function as a stressor to enhance tissue senescence and ageing, which in turn drives post-infection tissue remodelling. Although definitive evidence is still currently lacking, acute infection may shift the host towards a state of premature biological ageing and shortened health span or even life span, by possibly engaging multiple hallmarks of ageing, including chronic inflammation, DNA damage, telomere attrition, epigenetic remodelling, cellular senescence and so on. Nevertheless, this may help explain why a single infectious insult can produce persistent, systemic or multi-organ chronic consequences long after pathogen clearance. Vaccine efficacy beyond acute infection If acute infections can cause post-acute syndromes, worsen chronic dis- ease, initiate new chronic illness and accelerate biological ageing, then anti-microbial agents and vaccines must confer benefits that extend far beyond the prevention of immediate illness.
